The child care tax deduction of $1,000 for working mothers has not been adjusted since 1976, even though child care costs have soared to $2,500 a year in government-subsidized centres and even higher in the private sector. That the $1,000 tax deduction limit for child care which working mothers can now claim be increased to reflect the legitimate costs of child care which are currently running on average at four times that amount.

subsubtopic: FUNDING FOR NATIVE WOMEN'S FIGHT FOR JUSTICE AND EQUALITY-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, all sides of this House have recognized the blatant discrimination against native women in Canada and the urgent need for action to end it. Above all, native women need a strong organization of their own to represent their interests at local, provincial and national levels. A consultation process with the Native Citizen Directorate identified several areas for expansion of the native women's program, and a cabinet submission was to be made in early March. However, nothing has happened, and the Native Women's Association of Canada has not been able to obtain a meeting with the Secretary of State (Mr. Regan) to discuss their needs. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Miller):
That this House instructs the Secretary of State to arrange an early meeting with the Native Women's Association of Canada in order to arrange an adequate funding program so that native women will have the means to fight for justice and equality.

Whereas the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Lumley) has now publicly rejected the majority report of the House special committee inquiring into the formation of a national trading corporation and has, instead, joined with my party and the great majority of Canada's exporting business sector in opposing such a hybrid trading corporation, I move, seconded by the hon. member for York North (Mr. Gamble):

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. The devastation caused by the recent floods in Nicaragua and Honduras has left thousands homeless and without food and clean water. Many roads and bridges have been washed away, and the risk of epidemics is high. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton):
That Canada render to Nicaragua and Honduras all possible emergency assistance in this very grave situation, and that, in so doing, due consideration be given to the longer term development needs of these two countries.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce who, I am sure, is aware that the bank rate has just been set at 15 7/8 per cent, up about .5 per cent from last week. subtopic: MOTOR VEHICLE FUEL CONSUMPTION STANDARDS ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will not take up too much time of the House since this bill is probably one of the most useless pieces of legislation that has come before Parliament, certainly in the years that I have been here. One must wonder why it was part of the energy package in the first place because it is not certain, when reading the legislation, what it will, in fact, do. I will expand on that later. I will quote one sentence stated by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) just a month ago, on April 20,
Fuel Consumption Standards
during second reading in the House. He said, "This legislation, the Motor Vehicle Fuel Consumption Standards Act, was first promised in 1976". In 1976, Mr. Speaker! Does the minister not know that the situation has changed considerably since that time? Not only is this piece of legislation obsolete, it was not necessary in the first place. If the government was serious about creating energy fuel consumption, it would not be creating additional regulations at a time when the automobile industry is facing huge unemployment in the country.
May I say at the outset that if the government was indeed serious about further reducing the use of conventional energy, it would then encourage, through any number of incentives, the use of alternate fuels such as propane or compressed natural gas. Those are the steps that are needed by the industry. We know that this is not what the government is doing with this piece of legislation, or indeed with any other piece of legislation that is either before the House now or being contemplated by the government. The industry does not need Bill C-107, which is obsolete, unnecessary and in fact damaging, not only to the automotive industry but to the whole economy of Canada.
With respect to the automotive industry, surely this is not the time to burden further the domestic automotive industry. Instead, the government should act on the serious damage that Japanese automobile imports, for example, have inflicted on our economy if it wants to help the industry. I am certainly not a protectionist by heart, but under these difficult and unusual circumstances I believe the government should be taking a tougher stand with respect to imposing Canadian content regulations of offshore imports so that jobs would be created in Canada. The government has negotiated with the Japanese for two years and those negotiations have obviously failed. The Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Lumley) has accepted the fact himself just this week that negotiations are at an impasse. If his answer to that is those underhanded tactics in Vancouver which are taking place now and are creating further unemployment for Canadians, that is certainly not the step to take either.
If the government is serious about trying to help the industry, the second option is to create incentives for foreign investment in Canada. That is what is necessary to create jobs. One should know that there have already been 50,000 jobs lost in the automotive industry in Canada in the last two years. The situation is not getting any better at all, and here is a government coming up with a piece of legislation to put further controls, directives and regulations on an industry which is certainly already overburdened with regulations and other difficulties and is getting no support whatsoever from the Liberal administration here in Ottawa.
What Bill C-107 represents is not so much the Liberal government's commitment to energy self-sufficiency or its so-called made-in-Canada energy plan, whatever that is, because we know what is happening to its whole energy program,

June 3, 1982
Fuel Consumption Standards
although we do not have to dwell on that today. The National Energy Program has been a total disaster. That has been evidenced by the fact that the minister himself had to come before the House just this week to announce some new emergency measures. In those announcements alone there is an admission by the government that the National Energy Program has been a total and absolute failure. But the Alsands project has collapsed as well. Because of the tremendous increase in federal taxes, the price of gasoline has still increased, but not by the 18 cents a gallon which the Conservatives suggested in the last election campaign. Many think that the reason the Conservative government was defeated at that time was the 18 cents a gallon increase at the gas pumps. Canadians now know that the price of gasoline has, in fact, increased by nearly $1 a gallon since the Liberals made a promise that they would keep the price of gasoline to less than the promise made by the Conservatives.
What this bill, in fact, represents is the government's continued deception and use of empty legislation and empty promises devised to do nothing more than make the government appear to be doing something. That is exactly what it is. This is a piece of legislation that would give the government the right to implement restrictions on gas consumption by automobiles. But they are not telling us what those restrictions are in this piece of legislation. It is a vague piece of legislation which would create a threat to the domestic automotive industry without the automotive industry being able to plan ahead of time.
In his speech on second reading, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said that the industry needed "a long range plan to be able to plan ten years ahead". Well, certainly with this piece of legislation the industry cannot plan ten years ahead if this piece of legislation does not spell out exactly what the government intends to do next month, next year, two years from now or five years from now. So what is the minister talking about? It is empty rhetoric, that is what it is.
The reality of this legislation is that it is void of any content. Yet at the same time it empowers the minister to enact compulsory fuel consumption standards without indicating any specific details as to just what those standards will be or what the objectives of the government will be with regard to acceptable levels of fuel consumption.
The bill represents no digression from the government's reliance on those standards made compulsory in the United States, and it does not challenge their accuracy. That is a very important point to keep in mind, Mr. Speaker. The United States, which has compulsory regulations for gas consumption, has a standard to keep up, that is, 27.5 miles per gallon. We all know that the North American auto industry is governed by the United States and that the products are designed in the United States. The industry in the United States and in Canada is far surpassing the regulations imposed in the United States of 27.5 miles per gallon. Most domestic automobiles now get over 30 miles per gallon and some as much as 40 miles
per gallon. So why, Mr. Speaker, are we looking at this piece of legislation today, why was it included in the omnibus bill in the first place?
I pointed out at the beginning of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, that the minister said that this legislation has been in the works since 1976. It is just giving some bureaucrats in their ivory towers who know absolutely nothing about the automotive industry, and also obviously know nothing about the energy situation, something to put together, to give them the job of creating an extra piece of legislation.
This bill is not helping the energy situation, it is harming the automotive industry and it is not assisting Canadians in any way whatsoever. If fact, the minister has in mind regulations of a new type in this piece of legislation. I believe that these regulations should be spelled out before any such legislation is passed by the House. That is exactly the point I am trying to make, that we cannot trust this government, we cannot allow it the opportunity to do to the automotive industry, by fuel consumption regulations that might be unrealistic, what this government has done to the energy industry with the National Energy Program. I do not want to dwell on the disaster that the National Energy Program has caused to the economy for all Canadians.
In fact, the minister has in mind enacting standards that are already being met and surpassed. It would amount to nothing more than demanding, for example, that vehicles come equipped with safety belts, a feature that is already compulsory, in other words, reinventing the wheel, a waste of the time of Parliament.
I would like to take a look briefly, Mr. Speaker, at the practicality of this legislation. In 1976, when this legislation was put together, Canada implemented voluntary fuel efficiency standards for automobiles. That, Mr. Speaker, was in the post-OPEC oil embargo days. It is very important to keep that in mind. That was at a time of fuel shortages and at a time when North Americans were just beginning to swallow the hard medicine that fuel prices were about to increase dramatically. It was a time when energy conservation was fast becoming one of the primary objectives of economic planning. In that same year the government promised to bring forward legislation that would put into law those voluntary fuel efficiency standards that I have just mentioned. When one looks at this bill, Mr. Speaker, it would almost appear that its introduction now is nothing more than desk cleaning. The bill is empty. It does not deal with the very significant changes that have taken place in the automobile industry since 1976, nor with the vast changes that have taken place in the energy situation since that time.
I would suspect, notwithstanding the fact that most Canadians are wise to the methods of this government, and that they will be wise to their methods when the next federal election takes place as well, that one of the reasons the government has not been motivated to pass those fuel consumption standards that it promised in 1976 is simply that the Americans had already beaten them to it, just like interest rates. We are well

June 3, 1982

aware of the Liberal preference to have our policies determined in Washington. At the same time, I do not mean to underestimate the importance to the federal government of a matter such as this, they having already sold out our automotive industry. Given the size of our automotive market relative to that of the United States, regulations such as these would be a little like the tail wagging the dog. That, Mr. Speaker, is another reason why I question the minister's intention in attempting to push this bill through this third reading stage and through Parliament.
I wish to get back to those regulations already in effect by virtue of the fact that our vehicles are designed and tested in the United States. This goes as far back as 1973, I believe, when the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency initiated a voluntary fuel efficiency labelling program. This was superseded in 1975 by the passage of amendments to the motor vehicle information and cost savings act, which stipulates (a) the actual fuel economy standards to be reached for each auto manufacturer for 1978 to 1980, and until 1985; (b) the legislation requires that labels indicating the fuel efficiency of each car be affixed to the automobile; and (c) that the EPA must publish a book listing all efficiency ratings and that that book must be made available to all auto dealers.
On average, these standards are met in Canada by virtue of the fact that, as I have already said, these automobiles are designed and tested for this market, whether they are produced in the United States or in Canada. In fact, in Canada most vehicles, on average, surpass even these standards because our emission level standards, as everyone knows, are lower than those in the United States. The minister has not challenged these standards. The bill does not contest the accuracy of these tests, nor their applicability to the Canadian market.
So exactly, Mr. Speaker, what does the minister have in mind in asking Parliament for the authority to enact yet unknown standards? Why is the Liberal government trying to attempt to pass legislation without spelling out what the changes and standards would be? It is just more bureaucracy, and that is something that we certainly do not need more of at this very dangerous time in our economy.
Technically speaking, this Motor Vehicle Fuel Consumption Standards Act embodied in Bill C-107 only continues the conceit of the federal government, but with a new twist, Mr. Speaker. Whereas former energy ministers have maintained that we have fuel consumption standards when in fact none were in place, the present minister now proposes to implement such legislation but at the same time wants to pretend that he has no authority. If he had no authority, then he would not be presenting this bill; and if he had the authority, he would not have to present this bill and he would come up with the specific requirements now, so that this House and Canadians and the automotive industry would know what those requirements would be.
The EMR briefing note on the act claims that it would be a two-stage bill. If voluntary standards fail to work, a second part of the bill will allow the government to implement compulsory standards. But that is not what is written in Bill C-107;
Fuel Consumption Standards
and that is again why I believe we must question the intention of the minister and not allow this bill to pass.
The bill clearly gives the government the authority to set fuel consumption standards which the industry must meet at some time in the future. There is absolutely no mention in the bill of voluntary standards. In fact, there are only two very absurd ways the government could set voluntary standards under this bill. One would be to set standards by one regulation and by another to exempt everyone, a contradictory situation. The other way would be to set no standards at all.
Under those circumstances, why do we have this legislation? If the reality is that this government is concerned only with appearing to be doing something, I for one do not believe the minister should be empowered with this authority. If the government does have it in mind to legislate the same standards that exist in the United States, then I think there should be a clear statement to that effect contained in this bill, and it clearly is not there.
If the government does not have that in mind, I demand that this House be advised of the real objectives of this bill. Is there something hidden in this bill which gives the government the power to do something in the future about which neither we nor the industry know? It is not specified in the bill. That is why I question the bill.
I remind the government that the automotive industry has already demonstrated its intention and ability to respond to energy shortages. Fuel consumption has decreased dramatically since 1976, not because of bills of this nature but because of the considerable increases in the price of gasoline. The price of gasoline in Canada is going up when it is going down everywhere else in the world. If it continues to go up, we will have energy self-sufficiency by 1990 because people will no longer be able to afford to buy gasoline.
What, at its introduction, at its second reading and at committee stage, was vague legislation continues to be vague. Without content, it serves only to upset an industry which simply does not need to deal with the threat of yet more regulations, and the automotive industry employs more Canadians both directly and indirectly than most others.
I want to say in closing what I said when I began. If the government were really serious about trying to preserve conventional energy, it would encourage the use of alternate fuels. I have just mentioned two, and I will repeat them: propane and compressed natural gas. However, the government is not going in that direction. If the government were serious about trying to help the automotive industry, it would deal with the Japanese in a tougher way. It would deal in a realistic way with the automotive industry in order to protect jobs in Canada. It need not necessarily impose embargoes on offshore imports; it should be creating Canadian content regulations and incentives for foreign investment in Canada. I would not mind a Honda plant in my riding, as long as it was creating Canadian jobs and helping the Canadian economy. However, we cannot continue to strangle our domestic industry and impose further regulations on our domestic industry while

we allow the Japanese to send us $1.5 billion worth of automotive products and while we sell the Japanese nothing more than token windshield wipers. In fact, Canadian automotive products sold to Japan amount to only one half of 1 per cent of the total Japanese imports to Canada. That is not free trade, it is not fair trade and the Japanese are very much taking advantage of that situation.
If the government is really interested in improving our whole economic system, whether it be through trying to protect or help a specific industry, preserve gasoline or encourage productivity, the government has only one alternative, and that is to throw out that "tremendous" budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) of last November, which has been damaging to the economy of this country, and replace it with a new budget. Only then can we begin on a new road to recovery.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: MOTOR VEHICLE FUEL CONSUMPTION STANDARDS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate which marks the end of a process which began some time ago. It is nice to see the Conservative Party energy critic who has returned from worldwide travels. I welcome him back to the House and the proceedings. I include in that, of course, the energy critic for the NDP, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell). They both know we have had deliberations on this particular bill, heard witnesses before the committee, and then we debated it quite seriously.
This bill, Mr. Speaker, is an important part of the National Energy Program. It is a key conservation measure aimed at reducing the consumption of fuel by motor vehicles in Canada. I wish to remind hon. members of the magnitude of the oil savings we believe can be achieved by this program. The savings have been estimated at 300,000 barrels of oil per day by 1990, compared to the fuel required by vehicles maintained

June 3, 1982
Fuel Consumption Standards
at a 1979 level of fuel consumption performance. This represents a sizeable reduction in transportation energy use, the largest sector of oil consumption in Canada.
Our commitment to this program dates back at least six years, and has embraced a history of discussions with the auto industry as well as numerous Canadian and foreign government agencies. The result was a successful voluntary fuel consumption program, supported by Bill C-107. The importance of this bill and the large measure of agreement on its role was evident in its success in committee. The performance of industry under this voluntary program provides further evidence of success. The targets for fuel consumption performance have not only been met but exceeded to date, and it is our expectation that this trend will continue. This willingness and expressed commitment of industry to co-operate with us makes a good case for retaining the voluntary nature of the program.
As a means of enhancing this voluntary program, industry and the federal government will work together in many areas. Industry is certainly willing to participate beyond current levels and we intend to harness this co-operation in order to coordinate all interests affected by the Motor Vehicle Fuel Consumption Standards Act, including the fuel-producing industry. We hope to focus this effort through industry-government working groups, one of which will concern itself with fuel consumption data. My colleague, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), has had notable success in developing a reporting system which provides key reports to the government from industry which indicate vehicle fuel consumption performance, sales, and thereby incorporate average fuel consumption information. This system is central to the production of the motor vehicle fuel consumption guide which I am sure many hon. members have heard about or seen in dealer showrooms. I should emphasize, however, that this reporting system is designed to support the administration of the program rather than the formulation of policy.
We therefore wish to involve industry actively in the development of relevant data to support fuel conservation policies which affect them directly. I wish to take this opportunity to commend the motor vehicle producers for their expressed willingness to participate not only in the gathering and analysis of data, but also its interpretation.
I want to emphasize that the flow of information will be two-way. For example, we will provide the information the industry needs to project future fuel supplies and quality. We also recognize the research and development efforts which industry has made over the past ten years in order to respond to the rapidly changing market and energy conditions. Research on cold weather fuel consumption is a good example of this effort. The government realizes the burden which such efforts impose, necessary though they are in this day and age
of conservation. We, too, have an obvious interest in research and we will support industry's efforts.
In the vital area of motor vehicle fuel we will work with industry to determine the optimal mix of fuel and fuel quality for use by vehicles in the future. In this way we hope to be able to co-ordinate industry's reponse to new fuel options. There is a great deal of interest in fuel options and we have committed ourselves to examine these in detail and to strike with industry and provincial governments a consensus on what an appropriate mix and quality of conventional and alternate fuels might be and how they are best used in Canada in the coming decade.
Under this "enhanced voluntary" program our approach to the setting of fuel consumption standards will be one of meeting with the industry to secure a realistic picture of the constraints and opportunities imposed by technology and economics on fuel consumption performance. We will seek to obtain views on Canadian market demands and trends as well as fuel availability, quality and trends in other countries. We will also take into account other regulatory constraints on industry, such as emissions and safety. From that should come informed decisions on achievable, effective standards for motor vehicle fuel consumption performance, with appropriate credits for new fuels we may wish to encourage.
Through these negotiations, Mr. Speaker, through working groups and further discussions between industry and government, we hope to make clear our expectations for industry performance under a voluntary program. This commitment we see as being essential to continued mutual trust. The government has decided that the program will remain voluntary unless companies fail to co-operate. As with all government programs, we take quite seriously the process and need for regular analysis and evaluation of this program, especially in terms of its effectiveness in meeting its goals. We will be dealing with this in our annual report to Parliament under this bill. It will include an assessment of compliance with program requirements, and the impact it has on real world fuel consumption. We will be assessing the case for continuing the program beyond 1990, and for other approaches which may be required.
Again, Mr. Speaker, the key objective is to improve the flow of information concerning motor vehicle energy consumption. We are very pleased to find no reservations on the part of industry in responding to our desire for improved two-way communication. We feel passage of this bill will be a significant step toward energy self-sufficiency. We want to see this long-standing commitment fulfilled, and we will strive, in cooperation with other government agencies and industry, to ensure that the aims and objectives of this bill, an important part of the NEP, are achieved. In concluding my remarks I urge all hon. members to support this legislation.
June 3, 1982

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to add just a few words on this bill. I am glad that no member of this House had the gaucherie to mention that Members of Parliament beat the pages in last night's baseball game! I am glad no one pointed that out; it was a fairly close game.
This bill is really important and it has not had very much debate. It is ironic that we spend all our time debating taxes and grants to oil companies, etc. These are all things on the supply side of the equation-that is, where we get our oil and gas-and we spend very little time in committee or in debate on the demand side of the equation.
The parliamentary secretary who just spoke said that energy self-sufficiency is the goal of the energy program. But we should be talking about energy efficiency. As the hon. member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) has said, if we looked at our demand for energy we could really make some progress in energy self-sufficiency. The hon. member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. Rose) never ceases to point this out.
This bill deals with fuel standards for cars. Ralph Nader, the American consumer advocate who pushed fuel standards, would laugh if he read this bill. It is a very weak bill. It does virtually nothing. It sets out voluntary standards for companies. Consumption standards should be more stringent. The auto exhaust emission standards should not be sacrificed in return for better fuel consumption ratings as set out in this bill.
Fuel Consumption Standards
It seems to me that we should be talking about increased fuel efficiency and reduced pollution emissions. We should have better targets set up that are contained in this bill. The government should set its targets now as the industry is planning ahead.
This bill really does nothing out of the ordinary. It does not change anything that is happening right now. We do not set any tough standards for the industry. If we did we would give the industry something to shoot at. We have taken a second-rate approach compared to what the Americans are suggesting. Automobiles and light trucks consume about one third of Canada's refined petroleum products. Out of eight bills, is there very much in them dealing with conservation? We have something in part of the first bill and something in this bill. This bill is a Mickey Mouse nothing bill. It deals with fuel consumption standards and looks for voluntary standards. It does not set out any tough standards to follow.
It seems to me the government is making a mistake. It is another fault of the National Energy Program. In the future the government should bring in bills to deal with energy conservation that have some teeth in them so that we can get into the matter of fuel consumption.
A pattern is developing in Canada. Some of the major automobile companies are now starting to build fuel guzzlers again. I mean big cars, of course. To continue doing that will be a tragic mistake. People are beginning to think there will be a big oil glut on the world market. As a result, people are again starting to use oil and gas like there is no tomorrow. The minister said the other night we have made progress. He is right; Canadians are conserving fuel. But we have only begun to do that. We can do much more. I suggest to members opposite that they subscribe to and read a publication called "Canadian Renewable Energy News". I believe the editor's name is Mr. Jeff Passmore. I have been reading this publication lately in more detail and I have begun to realize there is a tremendous saving that we can still achieve in conservation.
We in the New Democratic Party are going to vote against this bill, not because we do not want fuel consumption standards for cars and not because we do not want to see energy efficiency, but because we want a bill with teeth in it dealing with auto exhaust emission standards and better fuel consumption standards, along with some guidelines for the industry. What Canadians need is a balance between the carrot-the advantages in price that conservation will give them-and a little bit of the stick. Canadians have to be pushed into conserving fuel. What better way to push them into doing that than imposing standards for cars, light trucks and vans which use one third of our refined products? But conservation in this area cannot be done with this bill.
This bill is typical of Liberalism. It is a halfway thing. The government thinks it is in the middle, the wishy-washy middle. Being in the wishy-washy middle is not leadership, nor will it give us energy efficiency in this country.

June 3, 1982

That an Order of the House do issue for copies of all government studies completed in the past five years concerning the use of generic drugs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is once again my privilege to be speaking in this Thursday five o'clock "happy hour", and the subject today is generic drugs and the pharmaceutical industry.
1 should say at the outset that I am no longer interested in obtaining a House order for the production of papers, it having been amply illustrated in this session that such a House order is valueless. 1 have illustrated that, despite a House order for the production of documents, there is no obligation on the part of a department to supply the documents referred to in the motion. In fact it is now abundantly apparent that until the House rules are changed, it is meaningless to obtain such House orders. Therefore, since I want to air a problem, I will continue as often as I can to use this opportunity to speak about the subject in question and no longer concern myself with trying to obtain documents.
When I was first elected in 1972 the very first call I received was from a Mr. Jack Fralich, who was then the president of Hoffmann-La Roche, a major Swiss-owned multinational pharmaceutical company in my riding. He wanted to see me about government legislation, Bill C-102, and specifically compulsory licensing.
Anyone who journeys from Ottawa to Montreal or from Toronto to Montreal will observe in the constituency of Vaudreuil a huge concrete monument to Bill C-102. That huge concrete structure, which was built at a cost of something in the order of $16 million, was to be the forerunner of a $65 million plant for the production and distribution in North America of drugs from the giant Hoffmann-La Roche company. The $65 million of 1969-70 probably would be at least twice that amount today. One can see how much has been lost in terms of construction and jobs because that particular project did not go ahead.

June 3, 1982
Generic Drugs
If one passed that huge concrete structure at night, one observed that only a limited number of floors had their lights on. In other words, only a limited number of floors were occupied. The rest of the floors were empty in 1970, in anticipation of expansion, but they remain empty today, in 1982.
One can and undoubtedly will argue what the benefits of compulsory licensing have been to the consumer, but I will let someone else deal with that subject. I want to point out, though, that in that one company alone, the loss of investment in Canada, the loss of jobs to Canadians and the loss of research and development have been very considerable indeed.
A few words about the industry are probably appropriate. The pharmaceutical industry possesses many characteristics which make it interesting to economists and a concern to the public. It is an industry which deals directly with the health of individuals and, as such, there is a desire to ensure that its product is readily available to the public, both in terms of price and quantity. However, to the extent that drugs can be extremely dangerous due to improper use-or because of their very nature-there exists a strong tendency to regulate this industry. Through its role in the health care field there exist external benefits to proper drug use and, as a result, it is generally believed that a competitive solution will not be optimal. The industry is highly research-intensive. It faces an inelastic demand for its products and has the sole purchasing authority resting with an agent other than the ultimate consumer of the product. These features make the pharmaceutical industry somewhat unique and should be considered when examining the economics of prescription drugs.
The demand for prescription drugs is relatively insensitive to price changes. The person prescribing a drug does not consume it or pay for it. The consumption decision is made by an individual who is unusually familiar with the quality of the product due to his role as a physician and the practice of drug firms of providing a great deal of information to doctors in the form of advertising and visits by detail men.
The industry believes that firms which are innovative earn high profits which encourage others to copy or become innovative themselves. A firm cannot rest for long on its past achievements. It must continue to innovate in order to maintain its market share. Although at any point in time the concentration rate may be high, with some firms earning monopoly profits, the entry rate into the market will also be high. Such competition from new products will cause prices to fall directly or indirectly via quality competition.
The industry is experiencing a much greater deficit in foreign trade than previously. In addition to this, the domestic industry is supplying a smaller fraction of Canada's domestic consumption than previously was the case.
In answer to one of the many questions that I put on the Order Paper, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) indicated that the estimated percentage of the total national health bill spent on drugs in 1976 was 10.5 per cent. That figure is interesting if we relate it to the balance of
trade in pharmaceutical products. In 1971 the negative balance of trade in pharmaceutical products was $50 million; in 1975 that imbalance had grown to $110 million and by 1979 the imbalance had reached $232 million. Once again, Mr. Speaker, those figures were supplied by the government, this time by the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais).
In Canada, patents are awarded for 17 years, although the patentee has exclusive property rights for only the first three years. After that period of time compulsory licences to produce can be awarded to other firms if it is demonstrated that the patentee has abused his patent. This is not the case with drugs; patent abuse is not a pre-requisite for the awarding of a compulsory licence. Since 1923, compulsory licences in pharmaceuticals could be granted to produce patented drugs in Canada. The 1969 changes to the Patent Act allowed for compulsory licences to import the generic equivalents to patented drugs. After the 1969 amendments to the Patent Act, patent holders have been receiving royalties of 4 per cent-I emphasize that figure, Mr. Speaker-of the total sales of licensees, which is far from a monopoly return.
The government's policy toward drug R and D appears to be contradictory. On the one hand that monopoly power is granted through patent protection in order to encourage R and D, and on the other hand monopoly power is taken away through compulsory licensing to induce lower prices via increased competition. In Canada, over 65 per cent of total R and D expenditures do not originate in industry and are therefore not subject to the profit motive. Some inventions cannot be readily copied, even in the absence of patent rights. Often the inventor possesses a head start in the application of the invention and possesses know-how concerning it which may not be readily apparent to outside observers. The inventor also has a head start in getting the ultimate product to market, which usually generates a certain amount of product loyalty among consumers.
According to the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, there are two criteria on which the performance of the pharmaceutical industry in Canada can be considered inadequate. These relate to its balance of foreign trade position-to which I previously referred-and the level of research and development expenditures locally. Although these reports claim that a multitude of factors could be identified, the major reasons for this poor performance are judged to be government policies and regulations concerning the industry.
It should be noted, Mr. Speaker, that here I am referring to reports of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. These reports claim that the 1969 amendment to Bill C-102, the Patent Act, was a major contributing factor to the decline in Canadian pharmaceutical research and development. The arguments in these reports do not differ with those discussed in the original research branch paper of March, 1980. As with other studies taking such a position, these departmental reports equate reduced profitability of selling pharmaceutical products in Canada with reduced profitability of engaging in R and D activity in Canada.
June 3, 1982

I should like to read an extract from a letter written by the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Roberts) dated April 29 of this year. The letter is addressed to me and in it the minister writes:
The government is very concerned about the over-all low level of research and development in the private sector and is actively pursuing a number of measures to improve Canada's performance in this area. We recognize the importance which a strong Patent system can play in encouraging industrial investment in R&D thus creating the appropriate climate for innovation.
A little earlier I referred to the first call that I received after being elected to Parliament from the then president of Hoff-man-La Roche. It is interesting that one of the employees of this company with whom I have had considerable correspondence refers to the company as follows:
-certain companies, primarily the ones with the best R and D productivity, are being driven into the ground by Bill C-102. The attitude within these companies, who have been responsible for the saving of countless Canadian lives, is becoming desperate.
Referring to Hoffman-La Roche he goes on to say:
-now operates far below its production capacity, has shelved plans for capital expansion and is now in the process of reducing staff. The organization is trapped between falling revenue and increasing operating costs, and, not to be forgotten, also trapped between generic substitution brought about by Bill C-102 and true innovative competition.
The writer, Mr. K. S. Hardy, an employee of Hoffman-La Roche, referred me to a very interesting editorial which had appeared in the "British Medical Journal" entitled "Generic Prescribing and the Drug Industry". The following quotation is particularly appropriate in relation to the pro-generic legislation currently in effect at both levels of government in Canada:
-generic substitution would be a clumsy and ineffective way of reducing NHS drug costs and one which might discourage foreign investment in the British pharmaceutical industry. Long-term, a worldwide trend toward use of generics could further reduce the pace and breadth of research by the pharmaceutical industry.
As I said earlier, this gentleman has written me frequently and many of the comments in his letters are particularly appropriate to the subject we are discussing this afternoon. For example, he refers to a competing company, Smith, Kline & French, which used to have a plant in Montreal but which has now moved out of the province of Quebec. He writes as follows:
The research intensive segment of the drug manufacturing industry is the most responsible for breakthrough drug discoveries. These breakthroughs can and often do result in vast savings to the total health care system and benefit society as a whole. As an example it was calculated that prior to the discovery of the anti-ulcer drug Tagamet, hundreds of millions of dollars were spent either directly or indirectly on gastric surgery, in-hospital care, lost man-day economic contribution, income taxes, etc.
In a letter of December 15, 1981 he writes that Smith, Kline & French were the discoverers of the breakthrough drug Tagamet and goes on to say:
Despite the well-documented proof of social contribution relative to its price, it is noteworthy that the productive research effort which gave birth to "Tagamet" has been rewarded with approval of several compulsory licences in this country.
At this point in time, the first imitator is introducing its generic copy of "Tagamet" barely 4 years after the introduction of the original discovery.
Generic Drugs
Because of its research productivity, Smith Kline & French has learned rather painfully that Bill C-102 penalizes the research-based firms in direct proportion to their research success.
Now, because of one major discovery, surgery, long hospital stays, mortality, lost taxes and other social costs have been so greatly reduced that the cost of the drug itself is a minor consideration and is one that has reaped monumental dividends to individuals, governments and society itself, not to mention the saving in suffering and human life. As Mr. Hardy says:
None of Canada's major trading partners employ compulsory licensing to import. Hence, it should come as no surprise that Canada is perceived as being a "hostile" environment. Such perceptions will not change unless compulsory licensing is abolished and a fair patent system is instilled which recognizes product protection.
One of our previous Members of Parliament who eventually became a minister was Martin O'Connell, the former MP for Scarborough East. If I had the time I would have liked to quote extensively from a paper which he prepared in 1978 but I will conclude by saying, as does he:
With the return of Great Britain to patent protection, Canada remains the only developed country with this unique discouragement to product innovation and manufacturing in the pharmaceutical industry. In both countries, compulsory licences to import issued to companies which have not incurred the costs of research and testing appear to have had a profound adverse effect on research-based companies. This is understandable when it is realized that it normally takes some ten years of research, development and clinical testing by the patentee before a new drug is cleared for sales and that it may soon be overtaken by a new discovery, let alone licensed to a company interested only in manufacturing the products developed by others. But one need not look only to the British decision; good and sufficient reasons exist in Canada to modify the nine-year-old Canadian system of compulsory licences to import alternative generic products.
Because of my cough and for other reasons, Mr. Speaker, I should conclude here. I think I have amply illustrated that whatever benefits the consumer may have received from compulsory licensing in Canada, the cost in jobs, construction and investment has been very high indeed.

Mr. Speaker, I might start by suggesting to the previous speaker that there are a number of brand and generic drugs which could be used to help his throat. Perhaps we can talk about that later.
This motion, Mr. Speaker, reads:
That an Order of the House do issue for copies of all government studies completed in the past five years concerning the use of generic drugs.
The surprising thing is that this motion is even required and that we have not by now observed the kinds of things the previous speaker talked about concerning the impact on the industry, the market share of generic drugs in Canada, what the impact has been on research and development and therefore on jobs, and, in particular, on the quality of pharmaceuticals provided for Canadians.
The word "generic" is perhaps a misnomer; in a sense, all drugs are generic. What we are really talking about is whether or not a particular company with a particular brand name has the protection which would encourage it to do further research and development and other things necessary in order to produce drugs for human use.

June 3, 1982
Generic Drugs
An important aspect as well is the question of the responsibility the Canadian government has in this area. Because of the number of government supported drug plans for senior citizens, the government is directly involved in the question of which drugs or combination of drugs, generic or otherwise, are covered. The critical point here, which the previous speaker was trying to get at and which caused him to propose this motion, is that the drug companies with operations in Canada would have a degree of protection, which they do not now have, and which would provide the stimulus for them to carry on their operations in Canada.
One of the first questions in a discussion on that subject is whether or not in fact, even with their operations in Canada, they are doing research and development here and not in other countries. As the hon. member suggests, that would mean increased employment opportunities for Canadians. There is no question that, with the changes in the patent law and with the loss of some of the protection the companies had before, there was a major shift in this area. In some way that in fact benefited Canadians. This occurred through an influx of generic drugs which could be very efficiently produced at a very low cost.
The question is whether or not we had the necessary standards of quality by allowing these relatively non-controlled sources of drugs to enter Canada. It is clear that in some cases drugs of poor quality entered Canada, drugs which did not have the beneficial effect they were meant to have when prescribed for a particular disease. One of the drugs which was discovered to be a problem was, of course, tetracycline. It is well known that the standards of that particular antibiotic when it was imported into Canada were well below that which would be expected either by a medical practitioner or the patient receiving therapy. There was a very serious question as to standards, and that to me is one of the most important aspects of this matter.
In addition to the standards, an interesting question is whether or not we as a government have been following the quality of those drugs. Clearly a responsibility the government has to the Canadian people is to ensure that the quality of the drug being offered in Canada is good. Recently we have had a number of examples, particularly in the area of pesticides, where the quality of different chemicals allowed into this country has not been acceptable. We have ended up accepting the word of independent companies which have been used by different drug companies for testing of products to prove they were acceptable and would not cause ill effects should they be used in a particular way. DDT is an example of that. DDT levels build up. It is difficult to get rid of DDT. DDT has detrimental effects. Thalidomide is another example. The testing process there was important. Testing of drugs to determine whether or not they are acceptable for human consumption is very important.
The federal government has a responsibility for drug standards, but it has not been seen to be completely effective in the
past. All of us would, I think, want to take a serious look at this. I would question whether we have been following in a responsible and effective way the quality and the standards of generic drugs that are imported into Canada. I suspect the answer to that question is no, that we have not. I know we have improved our assessment to some degree, but I suspect there is a lot more that we could do. It would be interesting to find out what studies we have had on generic drugs in that respect in addition to the economic effect.
None at all.

I hear the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) say none at all. That is the point.
I will come back to the main argument put by the hon. member who proposed this motion. We have to examine the viability of the industry to provide drugs for Canadians at a reasonable price. There are Canadians with certain diseases who require large amounts of drugs over long periods of time. These drugs are important to their health. The cost of them can use up a major portion of a family's income. This can put severe stress not only on low-income families but on middle-income families as well. It is not unusual for patients to spend $100 per month on drugs for long periods of time. There are drug plans in which patients can become involved. Most people who face long periods of drug therapy eventually are able to get into some kind of drug plan. If not, there may be some assistance through some level of government.
The NDP government has Pharmacare.

speechtext: Even the Tories have it.

papers, although I think that is important. We on this side would strongly support that initiative. We would like to see testing of generic drugs as well as a number of other things which the federal government has responsibility for in health care, on behalf of all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I am not sure how much time I have. 1 hear that we may be called out of this chamber to attend the Senate.
I do want to say a few words about the whole question of drug testing. The motion put forward by the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) calls for copies of studies done by the government over the last five years having to do with the use of generic drugs. I am not sure just how many of those kinds of studies there are. I know there is an inadequate number of studies, indeed if there are any, on the effects of drugs which are on the market in Canada. It is a fact that some drugs on Canadian pharmacy shelves have never been properly tested. They may be dangerous to the health of Canadians.
Information made public recently under the freedom of information act in the United States clearly shows that in the case of at least 16 prescription drugs presently in use in Canada, the Department of National Health and Welfare have not properly protected the health of the Canadian public. Health and Welfare Canada commonly authorizes the sale of powerful new drugs based on testing done by the drug manufacturers themselves. In our view, it is irresponsible for the government to rely on private companies who manufacture the drugs and sell them also to test these same drugs. This is an obvious conflict of interest in our opinion and is something that ought to be rectified.
The Food and Drug Administration in the United States has recently found cases of misrepresentation, fraud and falsification of test results in U.S. drug testing laboratories. One hundred and twenty seven laboratories have been found to be in violation. Forty three doctors were suspended and another 24 are under investigation. The FDA caught up with one doctor who had been making up results by picking EKG tests out of a garbage can and assigning a name to a test result. Yet the federal government refuses to change the law to require that drug testing be done in Canada and at more reliable locations than the drug manufacturers themselves. For instance, these tests could be done in our Canadian universities.
The present system for testing drugs has to be changed or we will see and hear more of the horror stories that we have witnessed with regard to some of the drugs that are now on the market. I refer to the near fatal experience of a woman in Oakville, Ontario. This woman had been taking the drug clindamycin. This woman was given clindamycin in 1973 for a minor nasal infection. Within a couple of weeks she was near death from colitis. In the years since she has had a series of eight operations, and most of her intestines have been removed. It turns out the company that marketed the drug, the Upjohn corporation of Kalamazoo, Michigan, carried out clinical trials in 1969 which showed the drug to cause colitis but did not inform Canadian officials until 1974.
Generic Drugs
With regard to drugs, pesticides and other hazardous substances, the government must recognize that it cannot trust the drug industry to tell the truth. It will simply just have to be more vigilant. This would involve implementing some inspection programs in Canada. It would be a matter of inspecting laboratories and looking over the shoulders of doctors who conduct the tests. The government must come to realize that the situation whereby people involved in the conflict of interest which I earlier described, where the drug manufacturers themselves do the testing, cannot continue any longer if the health of Canadians is to be protected.
We should have research conducted on hazardous substances, as I suggested recently in this House in a Standing Order 43, by a national hazardous substances research council or similar body through which we would have the confidence that tests were being conducted by an independent body whose only concern was to discover, in an accurate, honest and scientific manner, what the possible side effects of various chemicals in the environment or drugs on the market might be. If that were to happen, I believe the Department of National Health and Welfare could truly be said to be looking after the health and welfare of Canadians, rather than sitting by with an either naive or diabolical confidence, I am not sure which, in information provided from the United States about drugs that are on the market.
A good example of this which I would like to mention is the anti-nauseant drug, Bendectin, which is prescribed for pregnant women. This has been a subject of controversy for several years since it has been suspected, although not definitely proven, to be a cause of birth deformities. It is the only drug which exists solely for use by pregnant women in their first three and most vulnerable months of pregnancy. I might add that it is also made by Merrell Labs, the company that has been dogged by doubt ever since it marketed thalidomide in North America.
Bendectin has been on the domestic market for 23 years, but in recent years it has been plagued by suspicion that it is a teratogen, which in layman's language is a drug or chemical that causes congenital malformations and defects in human and animal fetuses. Two recent studies show a statistically significant increase in birth defects in children born to women who took Bendectin.
The first study, conducted by Doctor Jose Cordero, reviewed
250,000	births. This was done at the Centre for Disease Control in Atlanta. The study associates Bendectin with such defects as missing hands and feet.
The second study, which was released in September, 1980, by Doctor Hershel Jick at the Boston collaborative drug surveillance program, suggests that Bendectin is a moderate teratogen on the limbs. Doctor Jick's report indicates that something less than five birth defects might be expected for every 1,000 women taking Bendectin during the critical early stages of pregnancy.

June 3, 1982
Generic Drugs
We have spoken with Dr. Donald Patterson who has been attempting to get the ear of the Medical Association and/or the Canadian government on the Bendectin issue. Dr. Patterson believes that Bendectin should be allowed to remain on the market but should only be used as an anti-nauseant for nonpregnancies only. That is to say, for motion sickness, chemotherapy effects and so on. Enough suspicion has been aroused in the United States regarding the safety of the drug that patient package inserts are included with each prescription. These inserts contain information on the risk and benefit considerations involved in taking Bendectin.
The most that has been done in Canada is that Bendectin is now sold by prescription only rather than over the counter as before. But in all these cases, whether we are in committee or in whatever forum where we have the opportunity to question the government on these matters, we find that all the government can do is quote from tests which have been done by private manufacturers in the United States who have an interest in the marketing and promotion of these products. What we in the NDP say is that this situation cannot go on any longer. We live in a modern society which has a great number of substances, whether chemical or pharmaceutical, that we have to contend with. In Canada we are virtually at the mercy of people who have an interest in making profit out of the promotion of these substances.
This brings us right back to a basic philosophical argument. Are these substances to be produced for profit or for the health and use of the Candian people? We would like to see the profit motive removed from these matters, particularly from the testing of these particular substances.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roy MacLaren (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the hon. member from Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) for bringing to the attention of the House of Commons the subject of the use of generic drugs in Canada.
It is to the credit of the member that he is concerned about this matter. It certainly does concern Canadians who need medication, particularly those who need drugs for acute illnesses and the many who need them for the curing of chronic illnesses or keeping these illnesses under control.
In all such cases, those who need relief from pain and suffering greatly value the achievements of the drug industry over the last few decades. World wide, the pharmaceutical industry has developed, tested and introduced many new products with extraordinary powers to ease the afflictions which have burdened men, women and children for centuries. There is no doubt that these accomplishments have made a significant contribution to the progress of mankind.
I am sure that the hon. member for Vaudreuil would agree that people suffering from illness need these medications at a reasonable price, especially if they need them for a long time or even permanently.
The hon. member has asked about government studies completed in the past five years concerning the use of generic drugs. With respect to the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, it has initiated three studies in the course of the last ten years.

speechtext: With the little time available to the Chair, I have been able to take a cursory look at the motions and it would be my intention that they be dealt with as follows: Motions Nos. 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11 should be debated and voted on separately; motions Nos, 4 and 5 could be debated together and voted on separately.

Motion No. 1
June 3, 1982

That Bill C-103, an Act to amend the Petroleum Administration Act and to enact provisions related thereto, be amended by deleting clause 12.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is the first of the energy bills to be debated in this chamber subsequent to the Standing Committee on Energy Legislation finishing its work. That work was completed at approximately 12.30 this day. It speaks to the difficulty that the energy committee has endured under the special House order, where hon. members of that committee have frequently been required to be in two places at the same time. It is a pleasure to be standing here this evening with no sense that the committee is meeting simultaneously with the House and that hon. members will have to make a choice as to whether to participate in the hearings of the legislation before committee or in this chamber.
I think it is wise at the outset to remind Canadians that Bill C-103 is a consequence of the bell-ringing which took place in this Parliament for 16 days. Members of the Canadian public may recall that the Progressive Conservative Party quietly, over a period of one year, attempted to tell the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) that it was wrong to bring in the kind of legislation proposed in Bill C-94. It was legislation that had far too many topics inside it, legislation that the minister intended to be debated in this chamber and in this chamber alone.
What the minister of energy wanted the Parliament of Canada to do was to deny Canadians the right to be heard as witnesses before a committee. There was a democratic principle at stake, Mr. Speaker, and we won that democratic principle on behalf of Canadians. We have had a committee. But it is a tragedy that the House leader chose to bring forward bills for debate in this chamber at the same time as the committee was meeting.
That procedure is exemplified by the fact that Bill C-103 was reported back to this chamber, a 50-clause bill, with 11 amendments already accepted by the government. Those amendments were accepted because of the work done by committee members and the work done by witnesses before the committee. However, the tragedy of Bill C-103 as it sits before us this evening is that so little of what those witnesses told the committee appears in the form of amendments.
Mr. Speaker, this bill is still so bad that there is a temptation to move amendments on each and every clause, but there is a danger in that, because we have a limited time to debate and if we were to move so many amendments it would be difficult for the Canadian people to focus on what is wrong with the bill.
I say to the Canadian people, those who are watching at this moment in time and those who may read about our debates, that the official opposition, the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada, attended each and every one of the committee meetings.
Hear, hear!

We spent seven and one half to eight hours on many days. We examined, in the most minute detail, each of the clauses in this bill.
Petroleum Administration Act
Hear, hear!

We will stand in this chamber and we will vote for the proposed amendments. And we will vote against the bill, because it is still a bad bill. We would like to invite government members, Liberals who were elected in this country in 1980, we would invite them, some of the independent thinking members on the other side, to consider the wisdom of each of the separate amendments. We invite them to think over their responsibility to their constituents, their responsibility to this nation, and join with us through the amending process in making a bad bill at least a little bit better.
Experience has taught us in this Parliament, Mr. Speaker, that the squeaking wheel gets the grease, that power is the name of the game. Unless those watching this debate, or reading about this debate, care enough about the country to pick up a telephone or pick up a pen and communicate their thoughts and their feelings to those members, then experience tells us that they are not likely to change, for some reason best left to them to explain. They bow to the squeaking wheel of public opinion; they do not bow to logic; they do not bow to what is good for the nation. But if enough Canadians across the country pick up a pen, pick up a telephone, and communicate their thoughts and feelings to a Member of Parliament, they can tell them clearly that they should support some of these amendments.
I urge people to listen closely to the logic of that. If Canadians are persuaded, then time is short. This bill will become law sometime next week unless members of the Liberal Party of Canada who were elected to serve in this chamber can be persuaded otherwise by their constituents and, let us hope, by the eloquence in this chamber. Common sense dictates, the health of the nation dictates, that the amending process required for this bill continue.
I would like to put into context, Mr. Speaker, a kind of schema, a kind of report card, that people can use for measuring the wisdom of a proposed amendment. There are many ways to develop a way of measuring a topic as important as this. I am trying to make it simple, Mr. Speaker. I suggest that there are four criteria that members opposite should look at before they decide whether or not an amendment is a wise one.
The first of these is: does the amendment provide any increased degree of protection for the consumers of oil and gas and the products thereof? Canadians should realize that when they go to the local service station and buy a gallon of gas today, the price they pay at the pump is greater than the price they would pay in many parts of the United States of America if they were to drive south. It makes people wonder about the campaign promises to keep the world price below 75 per cent, when they can just drive south of the Canadian border and buy gasoline cheaper than they can here. If they are wondering, then they should know that on average 65 or 66 cents out of every dollar that they pay goes to government in the form of

Petroleum Administration Act
taxes. The gasoline they put in a car, that they pay a dollar for, is worth 35 cents. When they buy oil to heat their homes, it is a similar situation. This bill has many taxing provisions in it, Mr. Speaker, and consumers will pay. Your costs as Canadians will go up if you give the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources the authority that he wants to raise your taxes. So people should look at an amendment and see if it will help the consumers.
Second, Mr. Speaker, in the climate in Canada today, Canadians should look at an amendment and see if it will help this country with jobs. Tomorrow we get the unemployment figures. Last month we had almost 1,300,000 unemployed. That makes you look at an amendment to see whether or not it has the wisdom of helping this nation and the Canadian people to have a job, a job instead of an unemployment insurance cheque, instead of a welfare cheque. A job-that is what Canadians want. To this point the policies of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources have cost this nation hundreds of thousands of jobs.
On Monday evening the minister announced the injection of $2 billion into the oil and gas industry, and that was a clear-cut admission that the energy policies of the past 18 months have been bullheaded, badly designed and harmful to this nation. They cost us jobs. We can see that in a direct sense in western Canada because rigs are not drilling. Truck drivers do not have trucks to drive. Caterpillar operators do not have caterpillars to operate because there have been auction sales, and the Americans have come north to Canada and bought that equipment for less than half price. The American industry has boomed, and our jobs have disappeared. That is a consequence of the policies of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
People in Ontario and Chicoutimi who worked for companies which provided parts for vehicles have been laid off, but it is very hard for them to see that they have lost their jobs because-in part, at least-the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has led this nation astray, with the advice and consent of backbench members of the Liberal Party.
Those are the first two. Does an amendment protect the consumer? Does an amendment help us get more jobs? My third criterion for judging an amendment is its impact on the economy and, in particular, its impact on interest rates. With his policies the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has encouraged Canadian companies to go on buying sprees. He has encouraged them to borrow money abroad. Even today we have further evidence of the consequences of that distortion of the Canadian economy. Increased borrowing of capital has driven down the value of our dollar, and that has caused interest rates to jump one half of 1 per cent today.
Canadians sometimes have difficulty seeing that government is their competitor in the marketplace when they borrow money. When they try to get mortgages for their homes, mortgage money is being auctioned off, and they are bidding
against their own government. Their own government can take money out of their pockets through taxes as well as outbid them. The cost of borrowing grows and grows.
The federal government is the prime culprit in this country. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources told us last Monday evening that federal revenues would fall $25 billion short of his projection. If the response of the government is to go back to the marketplace to borrow that amount, interest rates will continue to rise. Small firms and farms will continue to go bankrupt, and people will lose their homes.
Energy policies are not the total cause of our difficulties, but they are a very important factor, and each and every amendment should be screened against that criterion. Will an amendment help bring interest rates down? If we do not have the amendment, will interest rates climb higher?
The fourth criterion is whether an amendment helps our democracy. In theory this chamber is a place for debate. In theory a committee is a place to examine witnesses and to reach independent conclusions. But in reality all of the eight bills in the present energy package attempt to transfer power away from democratic systems and into the hands of a small group, the cabinet. Those of us who work in the Parliament of Canada as elected members know the kind of schedules cabinet ministers have and the amount of time they have to examine any particular piece of legislation in detail. It is darned little, and each time a piece of legislation comes forward in this chamber, it is flawed. It is usually seriously flawed; that is a consequence of a process. Cabinet ministers are too busy.
This bill seeks to transfer enormously increased responsibilities to a minister who has already demonstrated clearly and unequivocally to Canadians that he cannot handle well the responsibilities previously assigned to him. Why in the name of sanity, when that is so unequivocally clear, would we attempt to give that individual increased responsibilities?
I would like to repeat the four criteria for an amendment. Does it protect consumers? Will it help us get more jobs? Will it help our economy and keep interest rates down rather than allow them to go up? And will it enable elected people to do their jobs and to be of assistance to the government in screening legislation and making it better?
I hope members of the New Democratic Party will pay attention to the speeches made by members of this House of Commons, because one of the real disappointments in the Standing Committee on Energy Legislation was that of the 31 or 32 members-I forget the number-of the New Democratic Party, we saw only one of them in those weeks of committee study. The remainder did not come and did not learn. Sitting in this chamber they probably still do not understand.
Should we have a quorum count now when there are only two members of your party in the House?

speechtext: Order, please. The Chair has made every effort to watch the problem resolve itself rather than attempt to rule on it. Mr. Speaker, Motion No. 1 deals with the minister's decision, through a ways and means motion which was never approved by this House but simply approved by cabinet and the minister, to put a tax on aviation and marine fuel. That tax existed for nine months. It brought revenues to the federal government from the aviation side of the transportation industry. In the process of collecting that tax the government discovered it had an international agreement with other nations and that the tax ran counter to that agreement. The testimony from the minister is clear and unequivocal: that tax will be rebated to international air carriers but will not be rebated to Canadian air carriers.
I want the House to visualize just how unfair and unjust that is for consumers, for employment, and for our economy generally. For example, Wardair, a Canadian-owned air transportation company, does 98 per cent of its business on international routes. The Canadian government has decreed

June 3, 1982
Petroleum Administration Act
that in the industry, when Canadians compete with a Russian, French, British or American airline flying from a Canadian airport to an airport in another country on the same route, the Canadian company shall pay 25 per cent more for fuel in this country than those foreign carriers.
That defies logic, it defies common sense, and it hurts. The airline industry in Canada is laying people off. Recently Air Canada reported a $27 million loss. It is an interesting coincidence that its increased tax bill was $26 million.
What the government decrees in Clause 12 of this bill is that Canadian companies shall be rendered non-competitive relative to foreign companies that fly in and out of Canadian airports. That is the first reason why this amendment to delete the clause should be supported. If the House were to vote to delete that clause, then the government would have no choice but to rebate the money to Canadian air carriers and thus treat them in a fashion consistent with the way carriers of other countries are treated. Where is the logic in penalizing a Canadian company and offering a bonus to a foreign company that competes with us?
The government says that a Canadian airline that flies from Canada to New York shall pay more for its fuel than the same size airplane on American Airlines which flies exactly the same route. That is insanity. It is a prescription for bankruptcy, a prescription for job loss. It is insanity. I defy any member of the Liberal Party who sits in this chamber to defend the logic of penalizing a Canadian company and bonusing a foreign company that is in direct competition on the same route. Hon. members opposite should stand up and give one sensible reason why any member of the House should vote for that principle.
Let us consider what we were told by the marine industry, Mr. Speaker. There are 17 ships at berth that have no cargo; they are sitting idle. We were told this is because these provisions have increased their costs to the point that they cannot compete with alternate modes of transportation. Two thirds of the cargo which our Great Lakes shipping fleet has traditionally carried from American producers to Baie Comeau for shipment around the world, has been lost for one reason, and that is the federal government's determination to collect a special tax from our shipping industry. That is the consequence of Clause 12, Mr. Speaker. We were told that the amount was $5 million, but the loss in Seaway tolls is $4 million and the loss to companies in increased paper work is at least $500,000. That is without even considering that if the sailors were employed and paid income tax, more revenue would be generated.
That is the consequence of Clause 12, Mr. Speaker. It gives me pleasure to move that it be deleted. I would remind hon. members that to support the motion would be to remove the discrimination that has cost so many jobs and has increased the cost of airline fares and cargo. It works its way through the economy, Mr. Speaker. We develop a transportation network that works reasonably efficiently when we allow transporters to compete. We have trucks, we have trains, we have ships, and we have planes. In his wisdom the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, not the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), has
said that two elements of the four shall be made non-competitive. Why did he pick on ships and planes? The answer we got in committee was because it is administratively easier to tax ships and planes and the fuel they use than it is to tax trucks or trains-no economic logic, no consideration of the repercussions on jobs and costs; simply that it is administratively easier to collect a tax from those two elements of our shipping industry.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, hon. members will discover in other amendments and motions that the same lack of logic, the same harmful consequences exist. 1 urge members of the Liberal Party in particular, perhaps in caucus or in some special committee, first to learn about these amendments, why they have been proposed, what they would do that would be good for this nation, and then mount a lobby group. We watched the lobby over the concerns to Hydro-Quebec and Ontario Hydro, and it worked. The minister changed what the members wanted him to change. I invite them to form a similar lobby to support this party in passing the amendments we have proposed and which they think make sense.
I look forward, Mr. Speaker, to a member of the Liberal Party standing in this chamber and telling me why this first amendment does not make sense. All it seeks to do is to treat aviation and shipping in a manner consistent with the way we treat trains and trucks. It further seeks to treat a Canadian company as well as we treat a foreign country air carrier. It provides no special advantage for the Canadian carrier; it simply takes away the disadvantage which the minister said Canadian carriers must bear. We must do that as quickly as we can, before those carriers face bankruptcy.
