I talked to Colin Park, who is manager of the oil division of Seaspan International Ltd. which does 95 per cent of the ship bunkering in Vancouver, and he told me that his company's business is down 25 per cent as a direct result of the price difference.
Tom McGrath, president of the seaman's section of the CBRT on the west coast, is a well known labour leader. He is very colourful. He is very quick to pick up issues on the coast which hurt his membership and ordinary workers on the west coast. Mr. McGrath confirmed that the problem has meant unemployment for his members.

You have to realize the B.C. government has also imposed a tax on bunker fuel in the amount of $5.66 a barrel. When the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) stood in the House many months ago to introduce his infamous budget, it not only caused the downfall of the dollar and seriously affected businesses, farmers and home owners who cannot afford homes, but also caused his own political downfall. His hair that was fluffed and blown when he used to enter the Chamber is no longer blown or fluffed; it is flat on the top of his head like his political future because of that budget of November 12.

Napoleon's retreat from Moscow many years ago seems like an orderly progression compared to the retreat of the Minister of Finance.

1 cannot think of any better example of the lunacy of those parts of the National Energy Program which are lunatic than the transportation fuel compensatin recovery charge which has no capacity to change even though the circumstances have changed. We know that the price of gasoline in Canada is higher than in the United States. It is lower in the United States than in Canada. Yet we have this ridiculous situation in terms of equity that if one is a Canadian air carrier or Canadian lakeboat shipper, one has to pay the increased tax levied two years before when our prices were high and American prices were low, whereas the American air carriers and lakeboat operators do not have to pay this tax today.
That is not my evidence or opinion. The most pertinent evidence before the committee was heard as recently as Tuesday, May 18, at which time not only the Canadian Air Transport group appeared, but also Admiral Timbrell and the president of the Air Transport Association of Canada, Mr. Angus C. Morrison. Sandy Morrison is a very interesting Canadian who has had some history in Ottawa. There are some people in this chamber, and perhaps even the Chair, who remember when Sandy Morrison was an executive assistant to one of the ministers of transport at some other time.
Sandy Morrison is a great individual. I know him very well, I would not suggest that he was a political colleague of mine, to say the least, yet he is now president. I can understand why he is the president of the Air Transport Association of Canada. He knows many people in Ottawa. So be it. I am prepared to face that reality. If another party is in power for 40 years, there will be other Sandy Morrisons. That is fine, too. That is the name of the game, to a point. But Sandy-Angus C.- Morrison is President of the Air Transport Association of Canada. Even the ex-whip of the Liberal Party, the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Lefebvre), who was over here a moment ago, will, I think remember Mr. Morrison. Mr. Morrison has said, as I said earlier, that this transportation fuel compensation recovery charge, in today's climate, is a discriminatory charge against domestic air carriers. It is not simply discriminatory. I want to show the lunacy of the situation under this charge which was levied against all air carriers.
I want to deal with the air carriers and the marine carriers under this charge. As set out in the evidence before the energy committee, and by the minister and his officials in the Transport committee, the domestic carriers and the Air Carriers International have had to pay several millions of dollars under this charge.
When it was levied, the Government of Canada, this present government, was warned that it could not levy a special charge for fuel against international air carriers because that would do one of two things. It would breach the bilateral agreements between countries, or it would run straight in the face of the air associations around the world as it would breach their agreements.
Does Your Honour know what has happened and what makes this matter so idiotic? The United States said that the
Government of Canada was levying a discriminating charge against international carriers, that it was unfair and that it would take the matter to wherever disputes are resolved, to arbitration within the system. Mainly because of this, the Government of Canada reluctantly said, "Do you know something? You are right. It is discriminatory".
We are not referring to several thousands of dollars, but, rather, many millions of dollars. To try to be as accurate here as I could, I was going to say $54 million domestically, and $50 million internationally. It is fairly close to that, and I could stand to be corrected. But let us say that the international carriers have said, "Hey, Government of Canada, under that discriminatory tax, you owe us approximately $50-odd million in rebate".
Lo and behold, because the Government of Canada was caught out in left field, it notified External Affairs which notified all the relevant embassies to say, "Please get the diplomatic couriers and an exchange of correspondence going so that a system or process could be set where we could pay back $50 million to the international carriers". Who is in competition with the international carriers in Canada but the domestic air carriers? We have now flipped this thing completely around from levying a tax against international carriers to ensure they paid the same for fuel that our domestic carriers were paying. They had to pay the same tax, under the breach of the IACA agreements and the bilateral agreements between Canada and other countries, flying into Canada.
Our government, because of pressure and because of the law of their agreements, has said, "Governments of the world, international government, you are right. We will have to pay back that $54 million in fuel compensation taxes." Yet, what is the situation with the domestic carriers? The domestic carriers have still been levied and have paid part of the debt of $50-odd million they have incurred under that tax. They have had no chance, and the question as to whether the government will pay back that tax to them has been turned down so far.
I do not want to get into the subject in depth because it is another law, but under another feature of the budget, which, in effect, I believe is Bill C-108, the government will not continue to charge the fuel compensation tax under Bill C-103 which, in effect, it has charged for two years. Under the tax changes which will eventually come up before the House in a ways and means motion, the same tax with the same impact will be levied against domestic carriers as we have levied before under Bill C-103.
There is the absolutely ridiculous situation involving domestic carriers. We all know how the air traffic industry today is in a very bottom line, almost thumb-sucking, very uncertain situation in trying to stay above the line between red and black. Yet, because of a direct policy of this government under Bill C-103 and the fuel compensation tax, which perhaps started off with some reason but which had no capability of changing when the circumstances changed, we are left in the ridiculous situation that if hon. members in the government vote against the amendment, they are voting to keep in place

discrimination against domestic and international carriers. That is what will happen if government members feel compelled to blindly support the government as they so often do.
I would like to refer to the other element, the marine part of this tax, and the interesting discrimination which will be incorporated in legislation, if this amendment does not carry. If I were a betting man, I would guess the odds were that it may not because the numbers are not on this side.
If I were a member from Ontario, especially a member from the Lakehead or an area joined to any lake system, I do not see how I could even begin to support that feature, Bill C-103, and allow the fuel compensation tax to stay because it also discriminates against the lake carriers. Today, our lake carriers are paying this tax, even though they are in competition with the American carriers. Again, I wish the press, who sometimes lambaste Members of Parliament, would pay attention to what goes on in the committee and find out some of the evidence, because I must say that I am a little jaundiced about what goes on in committee, the waste of time there, the hours and hours. But at least committees do collect a lot of interesting evidence and they are repositories of a lot of evidence.
What I said here earlier about the marine fuel compensation tax were not my words. They were the words of Admiral Timbrell, who happens to be-like Angus Morrison was the President of the Air Transport Association-the president of the Dominion Marine Association.
It is interesting for those members from Ontario especially, and even from Quebec, because they are affected by the evidence that Admiral Timbrell gave in that committee. He said, amongst other things, that his association represents 19 Canadian companies, that they have approximately 172 ships, or over 90 per cent of the Canadian fleet of large ships, 1,000 tons and greater. He said:
We operate principally in the Great Lakes and down the St. Lawrence and outside, coastal and occasionally deep sea.
They basically are a St. Lawrence operation. He says again in his evidence, interestingly enough, on May 18, reported at page 20:26 of the committee minutes of proceedings:
In an average year, we move about 90 million tonnes of cargo. To put it in perspective for you, we carry more in eight and a half months, which is our operating season, because of freeze-up, than Canadian Pacific rail does in twelve and slightly less than CN. About 50 per cent of our cargoes are foreign or are on international trade.
We know, of course, that CN and CP carry an awful lot of cargo. He mentions the twofold nature of the competition- with the United States and also competition in Canada. They compete against rail, they compete against bus, and those people do not pay the fuel compensation tax. He points out here, in a most interesting way:
When the charge came on May 1 last year and until January 1, my companies had paid the equivalent or approximate sum of $5 million in the TFCRC. That $5 million on our international trade represented an increase of approximately 6 per cent on our charges.
He says that in addition there was a $500,000 bill for administration charges. In terms of the tight competition

between the Canadian lake carrier and the American lake carrier, it is the evidence, according to the admiral, the president of the Dominion Marine Association-not me, not our party, but the president of the Dominion Marine Association that represents a conglomerate of Great Lake shipping, Upper Canada Lake shipping and Paul Martin's company. One of those is Paul Martin's company-another interesting Canadian who certainly has had an interesting political background.
All these gentlemen, regardless of their political background-that is the point-have said that this tax is discriminatory against Canadians trying to service the international market and/or the domestic market. He pointed this out here in a most interesting way. Perhaps I should read this for members opposite who were not privileged, as most of us were not, to be there at the committee hearing. He talked about the shipment of grain and how his association was so involved in grain, and how Canada gets the benefit of that traffic. He said as follows:
Last year, an average year, we carried approximately 6 million tonnes of U.S. grain to the lower elevators. We charge approximately $10 a tonne, so there is $60 million U.S. we collected for moving that grain. For each load of grain that went through the seaway, the seaway collects approximately $21,000 out of a $25,000 bill. The other $4,000 is for a ship. So, for every cargo we do not take through the seaway, they lose $21,000. If that grain, the U.S. grain, does not arrive at our lower elevators at places like Baie-Comeau Port-Cartier, Three Rivers, Quebec, Montreal, then those elevators, which are Canadian investments, lose an equal amount.
He is saying, and he gives the figures, they have been losing that amount. If for no other reason than that, in terms of the fuel compensation tax, which is a discriminatory tax against Canadians in competition with Americans, 1 would ask members of this House, before they blindly vote the party line, to try to sort out some of this energy problem and, in terms of Bill C-103, vote for the amendment that we have moved in Motion No. 1. That motion is clear, simple but strong, and it says "delete the fuel compensation charge under Bill C-103, primarily because the circumstances have changed."
If we could move there, Mr. Speaker, that, and another whole speech I could give, might show Canadians outside the chamber that this chamber and members in it are a little responsive to some of the problems in reality in the economy. There is just no logical reason why domestic air carriers in Canada should not be refunded the same as international carriers, when the two carriers are in competition with another; and there is even less reason why our Canadian lake shippers, in competition with their American colleagues and competitors, should still be charged a fuel compensation tax when their American competitors are not.
That is discrimination. That is not equity, and that is why, Mr. Speaker, I conclude by saying that the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) is in the appropriate place tonight, in the palace of Versailles, in the palace of mirrors, because this whole budget is a mirror and this Bill C-103 and the fuel compensation tax is one of the most distorted mirrors in the energy scene.

Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to add too extensive a discussion on this first motion, as I understand we will have many chances tonight to speak to this bill.
First of all, I am particularly concerned about the amendment in front of us, presented by our party. This is a simple motion, to delete this clause altogether. My colleague who spoke immediately before me said he was not in the committee. I was fortunate to be in that committee, to hear the pleading of the witnesses. 1 wished that the minister could have been there to listen to those witnesses.
I would like to refer particularly to one gentleman who with total dedication got a very strong point across. That is Mr. Currie of Wardair. The point that he brought out for us so clearly dealt with this clause. It is that Wardair is the only privately financed airline that is not either government owned or connected with a large financial institution. They have a debt to the Canadian government of S8.5 million.
Wardair is an airline that goes back in history to Yellowknife, to the Northwest Territories. A gentleman called Max Ward had the guts and the entrepreneurial spirit to start something Canadian, privately financed. This gentleman announced and brought out their first quarter earnings, showing a loss, because they have to show a liability of $8.5 million.
Let me compare that to KLM or British Airways or other foreign carriers which operate out of Canada. They got their money back. But Max Ward of Wardair did not get his money back. He is a Canadian, he is being discriminated against, according to the Constitution that the Liberal members are so proud of. There is something wrong when a Canadian citizen is discriminated against compared to foreigners. That is my stand for getting rid of this Clause 12.
Another point in regard to air transportation is that Mr. Lindsay, a vice president of the Air Transport Association and in charge of government affairs-I am sure he is a long-time friend of the government-gave evidence on May 18.
He said right at the beginning that Air Canada was making a profit, and Mr. Currie referred to why it was making a profit. At that date he stated Air Canada was making a profit. How can a vice-president of the Air Transport Association of Canada one day say Air Canada is making a profit and a week later the financial statements show Air Canada lost $27 million? Air Canada had to pay $26 million of it back to the government. I do not feel badly about Air Canada because whether it has a profit or a loss, it all ends up back in the same government pot. It is strictly a question of bookkeeping, and I would say the minister is probably a genius at manipulation of numbers, so it does not worry him, but it worries me because a man like Max Ward and Wardair are being discriminated against under this act.
1 would now like to turn to the Dominion Marine Association and Rear Admiral Timbrell, who I found to be a very clear-thinking witness. He gave us a great deal of information. What he impressed upon me was that we do not have many industries in this country which are really Canadian. We
cannot call the automobile industry Canadian. We can call the steel industry Canadian; my comments will reflect that. However, Rear Admiral Timbrell pointed out that what the government is doing is removing a benefit to a Canadian carrier. We could call it a non-tariff barrier, which every country in the world provides, but by removing this benefit, the government has put 17 ships out of business. Seventeen lake boats are out of business. They employed 500 people with a capital investment of $535 million.
This industry has always had a difficult time. It has never had a decent break from the government. I acknowledge that the shipbuilding industry has, but these people have not. They pay the price. They could buy their ships offshore, and the Canadian government would have to offset that by giving grants to the shipbuilding industry so it could compete with Japan, Taiwan and other countries, but this industry does not even have the advantage of the airline industry. It pays $40 million per lake boat, and it must finance that with money at 17 per cent to 20 per cent under this current administration.
We should encourage an industry which is purely Canadian and which has been successful, in spite of lack of incentives. Last year alone the industry paid $5 million in taxes, but this year it will lose $40 million in revenues. That is very bad thinking on the part of the government. It has prevented boats from travelling through the seaway, where the government could collect approximately $2 million. Five hundred people are now in the ranks of the unemployed. They are collecting unemployment insurance, and the government is not collecting any taxes from them. An interesting point is that these people are not low paid. The average wage on a boat is $30,000. The reason for that is the hours are 24 hours a day for eight months, and they take their holidays in the winter. These men are not paying taxes this year. They are among the 1.750 million people unemployed in the country, and I am including the 500,000 who are not even in the statistics. When we work out what the tax on their income would be, we find that it comes to in excess of $2.5 million. Then when we add to that the fact that these gentlemen are not able to buy anything because they have no income, we see that the government loses out on sales tax. The one I would like to mention in particular is the 24 cents excise tax on gas. There is also the 4.5 cents tax to buy Petrofina. So this sum of money is increased by another $1.5 million. As I calculate it, the government is out millions because of its being punitive to a Canadian industry.
I strongly urge that this House consider this motion and vote for it because the tax with which we are dealing is punitive. It benefits foreigners. It allows them to take our airline business away from us and allows American railroads, the American shipping industry to take grain shipments away from us via the Mississippi. I plead with the backbenchers of the Liberal Party to support this motion, especially if they want to get back into this House the next time around. Canadians are hurting. Jobs are needed. I plead with you, Mr. Speaker, as one of the members of that bench at times-you are not right now, but you are at times-to talk to your colleagues.

I would like to make one last point about a person in my riding. A small entrepreneur there decided it would conserve energy if transport trailers were shipped across Lake Ontario as opposed to going all the way around from Oshawa to Rochester. According to the information given to me by Rear Admiral Timbrell, it is some six times as efficient to go by ship as it is to go by truck. That gentleman started by going by carrier from Oshawa to Rochester, but this tax is one of the factors which put him out of business. We should provide grants to gentlemen like this who want to conserve. Transportation by boat is three times more fuel efficient than transportation by rail, and it is Canadian, not American.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few points on Motion No. 1. It is incredible to me that this government would be in favour-which it will demonstrate if it votes against this amendment-of treating foreign carriers of Canadian goods or foreign carriers competing with Canadians more favourably than domestic carriers. Surely we should be encouraging Canadians to export and to be more competitive with other countries around the world. I refer specifically to agricultural commodities. Agricultural commodities are a very important earner of foreign exchange for this country. Many of our agricultural products come from the west. The bulk of grain exported to earn foreign exchange for this country comes from the west. Much of our country is land-locked, and it is important that we are capable of moving goods from the west efficiently to export positions. That usually means seaboards, either east or west, and it is important that Canadian carriers be as competitive as possible with the countries with which we compete for foreign markets.
To talk specifically about grain, we know there are American grain carriers on the Great Lakes. Those operators hire out and lease their boats to move grain. If we put Canadian carriers into a position where they are not competitive with American carriers, that puts us in western Canada in a very precarious position in terms of exporting our grain. I just cannot believe this government would be in favour, by voting against this amendment, of giving an unfair advantage. Initially, the government imposed this tax on foreign carriers. It subsequently removed that tax and gave an advantage to foreign carriers over Canadian carriers. That to me seems ludicrous.
Let us look at what the European Economic Community does in terms of some of the agricultural commodities it produces. The EEC pays domestic producers of wheat consumed in the European Economic Community about $9 a bushel, which is $4.50 more than we pay here.
Instead of taking that into account and trying to be as fair as possible with our domestic producers, the government proposed a tax which puts our producers at a disadvantage when compared to foreign producers. I find it incredible that it would do such a thing.

The government has recognized that we have problems with rail capacity in western Canada and we have to give it credit for addressing that problem. But, Mr. Speaker, there is some unused capacity at Thunder Bay. However, this tax means that our shippers cannot compete with the Americans. It does not make sense to have unused capacity in one port and then tax Canadians at a higher rate than foreigners who carry our commodities. That does not make any sense to me.
The government wonders why it does not have any support in western Canada. Perhaps it should look for answers at some of the measures it brings before this House such as the one we are considering tonight. This tax will hurt our capacity to move grain to export and will make us less competitive with the Americans who are our chief competitors for world markets.
The hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Fennell) who just spoke pointed out that 17 carriers will be put out of business. I do not know how many of them will not operate in the present shipping season and I do not know how many are grain carriers, but even if they stay in business they will be at a disadvantage because of this tax.
The hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Now-lan) went over many points that I should have liked to deal with. 1 do not want to prolong the debate, but 1 should like to point out that if it is fair that the government should revoke and remit the tax paid by foreign carriers that burn Canadian fuel because of an international obligation, surely it should be incumbent upon the government to treat Canadian carriers in the same way. Essentially that is all the motion asks. Members of the government who vote against the motion will really be voting in favour of discriminating against Canadian carriers of Canadian goods. That will hurt us on the international market.
We have problems with the Canadian dollar and with interest rates. One of the ways to solve these problems is to be competitive in the export market. Yesterday the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) arranged to borrow $750 million on foreign money markets to support the Canadian dollar. Surely the government should instead encourage Canadians to export goods rather than borrow the money. If we can sell the goods that we can produce very efficiently, then we will not have a debt. When we borrow money, not only do we have to pay the money back but we also have to pay interest on it. This tax will discourage Canadians from earning the money we need to support our dollar and to bring down interest rates.
I find it incredible that the opposition should have to bring in an amendment like this one. If the government were governing in the best interests of all Canadians, it would not draft a bill like this in the first place.

Mr. Speaker, I will just take a few moments to reiterate the reasons for this amendment and to provide some reasons why members of the House, if they are to fulfil their responsibilities, will vote for it and strike Clause 12 from Bill C-103.

Clause 12 introduces a transportation fuel compensation recovery charge-a name long enough to confuse people as to its intent. That means it is confusing enough to deflect some of the political flack that should properly be directed at a government that would bring in what could only be described as an atrocious taxation measure.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and spokesmen for the Liberal party repeatedly claim to have done a marvellous job in designing an energy policy for this country. In particular they are concerned about the consumers of energy in Canada and, as an expression of that concern, they have moved to protect Canadians from the world price. For a number of years that has been the theme of the Liberal Party-that it is protecting Canadian consumers from the world price. That is a fallacious claim, Mr. Speaker. Any Canadian who lives near the border or who has travelled in the United States knows that it is cheaper to buy gasoline there than in Canada, even though the United States is at world prices.
We also know, particularly people in western Canada, that the policy means that the Liberal Party would rob the politically weak part of the country to give to the politically strong part of the country. This is all done in the guise of national unity with advertisements on television and so on. All the while the government expresses concerns about the growth of separatism in western Canada.
When you start monkeying about in the marketplace, whether you be the Canadian government, the Polish government, the government of the Soviet Union or any other, you louse things up. No central planning or decision-making operation can compete with a free market system which has the tremendous advantage of decentralized decision-making. That is one element which is absolutely essential to efficiency and effectiveness. When the government claims that things can be done better through centralized planning, it keeps making the same kinds of dumb, stupid mistakes-not through malice, not necessarily through lack of intelligence, except to the extent that it cannot see that central planning schemes do not work. They have never worked anywhere; they will never work because they cannot compete with the efficiency and effectiveness of the free market system.
The transportation fuel recovery charge is a classic example of this. For the brief period when we had cheap fuel in Canada, people started to take advantage of it. Airlines going from New York to Montreal to Europe found it made sense to fuel up in Montreal because of the cheaper fuel. They did not load up in New York. Truckers would enter Canada with an empty tank and leave with a full one, and ships did the same thing. It is understandable.
But the clever genuises who designed the National Energy Program imposed a transportation fuel compensation recovery charge. One day a piece of paper was tabled in the House and there was a new tax. The House was not asked about it. Members were not asked about it-but there was a new tax. But these clever little geniuses who designed this tax forgot to see whether in fact it was permissible, given our obligations
under bilateral agreements with other countries. Lo and behold it is not permissible, it violates some of our treaties.
That did not bother this government for awhile, the fact that provisions of the NEP violated our obligations under GATT and so on, and we have not seen the end of that yet. They are not bothered by any contract they sign with the provinces. Why should they be bothered by any of their international treaties? But then the Americans said they were going to take the issue to arbitration, and so the Canadian government caved in. How did they cave in? Well, through a little provision in the Financial Administration Act, I believe, which allows the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Rompkey) to rebate certain taxes. Rather than come out and be honest and admit they made a mistake-oh, no, no such admission-quietly, through this other provision, they are going to rebate the tax, but only to foreign international carriers, not to Canadian international carriers.
These same little geniuses have come up with a new scheme. They are going to do the same thing, but supposedly through the income tax system. It remains to be seen whether or not it will work. In essence, then, this clause concerning air transport is cancelled. It came into existence and then disappeared before the House of Commons had a chance to discuss it. It will not in fact ever apply to foreign carriers who will now have the full sum of $46.5 million rebated to them. It will only apply to Canadian international carriers. They will have to pay that $50 million.
This, Mr. Speaker, is the incredible situation we have. The House of Commons is being asked to approve a tax which no longer exists. It came into existence and disappeared before we even got around to considering it or thinking about it. It was introduced to supposedly prevent foreign carriers from taking unfair advantage of an energy pricing scheme which was supposed to protect Canadians from the world price, but which will result in Canadian international carriers paying the full tax while foreign airlines do not. Mr. Speaker, Rube Goldberg could not have designed a more stupid, insane and asinine scheme than this one.
It is incredible that anyone could come forward with this piece of trash and not submit his resignation. This is an affront to democracy, decency and common sense. It really is unbelievable. We must be a very docile people to tolerate this kind of thing. Frankly, I do not understand why Max Ward has not strapped some machine guns on those jets of his and strafed this place. The only reason this tax still applies to Canadian carriers is because Max Ward happens to come from Edmonton and does not have that much political clout. If he had been born in the minister's riding, we would not have this asinine tax; we would not have this silly and absurd circumstance where the House of Commons is being asked to retroactively approve a discriminatory tax, one which was supposedly to prevent foreigners from taking advantage of energy policies which are supposed to protect Canadians. There is no simple

Motion No. 2
That Bill C-103, An Act to amend the Petroleum Administration Act and to enact provisions related thereto be amended in Clause 16 by striking out lines 42 to 44 at page 11 and substituting the following therefor:
"ration of the parties, the Gov-".

Mr. Speaker, that amendment, standing by itself, is difficult to understand given that it contains two half-words "ration" and "Gov". The part of the act which this motion now seeks to amend reads as follows:
Where no agreement is entered into under section 22 with the government of a producer-province, or any such agreement is terminated by the declaration of the parties, or, in the opinion of the governor in council, is not effective or is not capable of being effective, the governor in council may, by regulation, establish maximum prices for the various qualities and kinds of crude oil to which this Part applies that are produced, extracted or recovered in that province.
If the amendment were to pass, Mr. Speaker, that section would now read:
Where no agreement is entered into under section 22 with the government of a producer-province, or any such agreement is terminated by the declaration of the parties, the Governor in Council may, by regulation, establish maximum prices for the various qualities and kinds of crude oil-
In other words, with this amendment the government of a producer-province may enter into an agreement setting crude oil prices if those parties agree they may change that agreement, or the agreement may be terminated. Without this amendment, what we have is a situation where the federal government unilaterally could terminate any agreement that it
Petroleum Administration Act
had entered into with a producer-province with respect to crude oil prices.
What we are trying to do through this amendment is to take out of the hands of the federal government the ability to unilaterally break a contract. Just on the surface, just from the point of view of common decency, convention, practice and established procedure, surely we should be able to do that. I like to think, I know it is naive, that Canadians and therefore the Canadian government can be trusted to keep their oral contracts. A promise made by any Canadian or by the Government of Canada should be kept. I would like to think that a handshake is all that you need to bind a contract.
With this government?

I know that is naive. It would probably put too many lawyers out of business if we ever followed that practice in this country, but it is not necessarily a bad thing. At least in Canada a written contract should be binding. A written contract should be something that binds and commits. Written contracts, of course, have force majeure provisions. That is, if some extreme event occurs, the contract may not be enforceable. That is understandable.
But to write into law and to make the law of Canada state that the federal government may enter into a contract and break it at whatever time and for whatever reason it wants is bad practice. It is bad law. More than that, it contributes to disharmony and difficulties in this country when a federal government breaks its word and breaks its contract.
In existence right now is an agreement between the federal government and the producing provinces for the price of oil. The agreement was effective September 1, 1981. But there was an agreement before that which was entered into in late 1975 for crude oil pricing. That agreement was entered into by the provincial governments and the federal government. That agreement called for an increase in domestic crude oil of $1 every six months. That agreement was to last until the end of 1979. However, in late 1977 as we approached what everybody thought would be the 1978 election year and the Liberal Party looked like it might be having a little bit of difficulty, the then minister of energy, Mr. Alastair Gillespie said "I am going to have to cancel the contract as it applies on January 1, 1978."
There was no other reason than that, Mr. Speaker. The federal government had an agreement with the producing governments. The constituents of Etobicoke said "We do not like our prices going up." Their member, the minister of energy said "Okay, I will cancel the contract. I do not feel bound by written contracts." The political considerations of the Liberal Party were more important than the honour and integrity of the Government of Canada. That is what the minister of energy did at that time. That is why people in western Canada are joining the Western Canada Concept Party. They say that they cannot trust the federal government to honour written contracts.

speechtext: The hon. member will have an opportunity to participate in debate. The hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre).

The hon. member talks about keeping one's word. He should read the rest of this bill. He will come to the part where 14 cents a gallon is mentioned as the maximum amount which the Liberal Party would allow gasoline to increase. If he does the arithmetic, he will find that 14 cents has suddenly turned into 52 cents under this Liberal government. That is if he is talking about keeping words and promises.
That violation of a written contract is only one of a series of those sorts of things. Is it not an insult to decency and to common sense and is this constant bickering between the federal government and the provincial governments not a concern to us? We should worry about the integrity of our country. This constant fighting has weakened us so much. Should we not be saying "If we are going to keep this country together and if we are going to have parts of this country feel like they are part of the whole, then as a bare minimum we have to have a situation where written agreements are honoured, kept and cannot be broken unilaterally by the federal government unless some extreme situation occurs which would be covered by a force majeure provision."
We should be outraged by the actions of the former minister of energy, Mr. Gillespie, in his unilateral violation of that written contract. We should be outraged and we should say never again will we permit a government to act that irresponsibly. We should not allow the government to show so little concern for integrity. We should not be asking the House of Commons to legalize that immoral behaviour. But that is what we are doing. The government is asking the House of Commons to make legal what is clearly immoral.
Last Friday the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was asked at a press conference when he will call the byelections for the three vacancies. The Prime Minister answered that legally he does not have to call those byelections for six months. The reporter asked whether he felt he had a moral obligation to do so. The Prime Minister asked "What is immoral about acting legally?"
He cannot distinguish between moral obligations and legal obligations. If it is legal, it is moral. His only moral code is the Criminal Code. If it is immoral to break a contract, as it most assuredly is-at least it has been in this country and has been part of our traditions because Canadians keep their word and do not break contracts-then the way to make it moral is to make it legal. That is the feeling of the Prime Minister and his party. If breaking contracts is legal, it is moral. That is what
members opposite are asking this House of Commons to pass. They want us to pass a law which would make it legal for the federal government to break contracts which would therefore make it moral, in their minds, to unilaterally break contracts.
Unfortunately, what will happen as a result of this legislation is that no province will enter into a contract with the federal government in which they will have confidence. The provinces will design their affairs accordingly.
There will be a continuation of the sentiment in the provinces of this country that the national government is a foreign government against which they should erect barricades because it is untrustworthy. There will be a continued balkanization in Canada. There will be the feeling in the different regions and provinces of Canada that the federal government cannot be trusted. Who can trust a government which says it will make it legal to act immorally in terms of honouring contractual agreements? Who would trust someone who said they would make legal what is immoral? That is what the federal government is asking for.
Although I know it falls on deaf ears, 1 would like to conclude by making the same plea. If the trained donkeys in the backbenches of the Liberal Party can screw up their courage, think about Canada and vote for this amendment, they will be serving their conscience, serving Canadian tradition and serving Canada of today and the future much better than by merely standing up and saying, "Aye, Sir, Aye" to the absurdities that continue to gush forth from the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources.

Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to speak on this amendment, but I do have a couple of things to say. I invite hon. members across from me to put up a speaker to reply because 1 think a reply is called for. I will try to explain why in a couple of moments. I noted that the hon. member who just spoke took a crack at lawyers and was supported by some of my colleagues.
From Brant.

If you are a lawyer, I suppose one of the things you learn in court is to try to put your case in such a manner that the judge or those judging it will accept it.
The hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) was attempting to make a case for his amendment to the government but spent 15 minutes insulting the government. There were a couple of remarks in the hon. member's speech which stirred me. He said that if Max Ward lived in the minister's riding, he would get help for his airline. I do not believe that this helps unity in Canada. We know what the implications are behind that statement. As a westerner, 1 do not believe that helps the situation.
The hon. member said that the federal government does not keep contracts. Although I do not like the federal government and have disagreed with the minister more than I have agreed with him, I have not seen the federal government break contracts in my experience. They have done many harmful things but they have not openly broken contracts.

June 3, 1982
How about this one right here?

I will come to that one in a moment. The hon. member for Calgary Centre said that the constituents of Etobicoke moved the former minister of energy to change an agreement. I would remind him that those same constituents voted for the member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) who is a Conservative. If the hon. member wishes to be in a future Government of Canada, he must reconcile the fact that the constituents of Etobicoke Centre want cheap gasoline and his western constituents quite legitimately want a top price for their resources. These two competing factors must somehow be combined in order to keep the country working. It does not help the situation for him to throw in these statements. They may backfire on him.
I find many problems with this amendment and the clause. I would like to hear more debate on some of the principles behind the clause. One of the principles is that oil prices should be set by agreement. They should be set by agreement because the provinces have control of their resources under our Constitution. They could set any price for oil and gas.
Inside the provinces.

That is true, but it would basically be better, as it goes to other parts of the country, that they be free to attempt to get the price they want.
I want a good price for western resources. If Ontario and Quebec are not prepared to charge proper rents and prices for their resources, that is their problem. We want good prices for our resources in western Canada. We still have the interest of the country in mind. Energy-Oil and gas-which we have been almost exclusively debating for two years is vital. It is important that we have a national energy policy.
If an agreement cannot be reached, it will probably necessitate a federal override. The federal government would have to set the prices but only after serious negotiations. We saw this happen in Canada when the federal government and the minister had to negotiate with Premier Lougheed. They eventually reached an agreement. Although many of us do not like the agreement-both the Conservatives and the New Democratic Party do not like it for different reasons-an agreement was reached. That is co-operative federalism.
One of the great tragedies which occurs in the House is not only when the hon. member for Calgary Centre insults the federal government about not keeping its contracts, insults electors in Etobicoke or the fact treatment would be different for someone in Quebec, we see the same problem on the other side with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). He said that cooperative federalism, is dead. He just likes to take everyone on in a fight, including provincial premiers and members of the House. This is not a good attitude either. He has not yet challenged me to a fight because he knows that he will easily win.
With respect to this particular question, what I believe must be considered is that once you have a contract, can you change it? The member from Calgary Centre said that the federal government can now break a contract at any time it chooses.
Petroleum Administration Act
That is not what the bill says. The bill talks about a contract being terminated. It says, " ... in the opinion of the Governor in Council is not effective or is not capable of being effected." The contract is not capable of being effected. The real weakness in this bill is what does that mean?
I am told that the French version is a little different. It refers to what happens if the contracts cannot be executed or implemented. That is a little different. Suppose we had a separatist government in Newfoundland or a WCC separatist government in Alberta or a tremendous change in the world and Canada was at war, or there was a great depression or something like that-
What do you mean, if?

-it may be that the federal government would need to have power to change the contract. We must surely have better wording and a better guarantee than that because we in the west do not want the federal government to unilaterally act like that. We say there may be periods or extra special occasions when it could make changes. Therefore, what I have tried to do is to set out how a co-operative federalism approach would work. I have tried to keep away from throwing insults at others on this particular bill. The minister was in the House a few minutes ago. I asked that an hon. member for the government speak to show us how this wording will not allow a quick unilateral action by the federal government to change an existing contract, because if it does, we on this side of the House could not support it.
I found to my shock that the recent changes in the National Energy Program update the other day were unilateral changes by the federal government. The change which Premier Lougheed of Alberta made a few weeks ago, giving $5.4 billion to the industry, although it affected the federal-provincial agreement at that point, was also a unilateral change. I think that is a very dangerous way to move. I will grant that the hon. member for Calgary Centre did say at the end of his speech that we do need some co-operation in this country. Therefore I say to the government in closing that when we consider this amendment rationally and in the spirit of co-operative federalism, and we must consider this clause, let us hear from government. Can the government tell us that the wording in this clause, which I think is defective in the English language and is somewhat different in the French language, will not allow the governor in council to quickly act unilaterally to change one of these agreements? I point out that while this may sound technical, we are dealing with something which is really important. It has taken up most of the debate in Canada in the last couple of years. It relates to the agreement between the federal government and the provinces, mainly Alberta, but also my province of British Columbia, and Saskatchewan. It concerns fixing the price of the most important commodity that we have, that is, oil. All Canadians feel that way when they go to the gas pumps to fill up.

June 3, 1982
Petroleum Administration Act
I believe I have made my comments in reply to the Conservative motion and I would like to hear the government reply to some of the points I have made, concerning the unclearness of the section.

Mr. Speaker, I chose to speak on this particular amendment because it is a critical amendment having much to do with the whole terms of reference and the way that the whole energy program, or, as one hon. member once alluded, the whole national energy problem, has been created by the legislation brought before us in this Elouse.
1 rise at this time following the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell). I do not know if anyone else could sort out exactly what he was saying. The one point we could take is that he was asking that a member from the government side stand up to speak. 1 think we understood that, but if the rest of what he said is any more clear to anyone else, perhaps one of the members could explain it to me, because I think he said that he does and that he does not. That may be all right in a courtship, but I do not really know whether the hon. member says he is supporting this motion or he is not.
Sit down and let him explain it to you again, if you cannot understand it.

The real question is whether the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway can read. Ele made an allusion to the French translation, and that may be well and good. But if he can read English, the statement is very clear, and he has been correct in picking out the part of the clause that we are trying to amend which states:
-in the opinion of the governor in council is not effective or is not capable of being effective, the governor in council may, by regulation, establish maximum prices for the various qualities and kinds of crude oil to which this part applies that are produced, extracted or recovered in that province.
That could not be any more explicit. I do not think there was any intent on the part of the government to either mean or state anything than that written in black and white on that page, within that clause. Unless the government accepts the amendment that we are honestly offering, unless it is prepared to say that it will not act in a unilateral way, it means exactly what it has said. I do not share the same confidence of the hon. member who previously spoke that the government had any intention to write anything else down there on paper or could in any way explain its way out of the intent and meaning of that particular wording.
It has been historically proven, it has been shown to us time after time, that the government is not only capable, but desires to have the ability and the authority to use its power in a unilateral way. It is as clear as it can be. It has repeated time after time in bill after bill in the parts of the energy legislation with which we are dealing today.
My main point in rising to speak concerning this clause is to consider it from the perspective of what will happen to consumers, to the people of Canada, by this particular clause in the reference. This legislation, this whole bill, is saying that the government will raise taxes. There will be two main taxes, one called the Canadian ownership charge and the other called the petroleum compensation charge. While the whole National Energy Program has fallen on the head of the minister, and
while he tries to justify an alibi and support the positions he has taken, which have been proven wrong time after time, we are now in a situation through this bill where Canadians are already paying 24 cents a gallon, roughly four or five cents a litre, if you like, for gas alone, for a petroleum compensation charge. This charge alone, right now, which is in excess, is doing all the things to consumers that the Liberal Party promised it would not do in the last election.
It is creating all of the increasing difficulties people are facing. It is increasing prices, hurting farmers, hurting commuters, hurting people who are using heating oil and who do not have any alternative. But on top of that 24 cents a gallon, which is already there, this bill and this particular clause gives the unilateral power to the federal government to charge an additional 24 cents a gallon at the discretion of the minister without agreement with the provinces. That would amount to a total of somewhere around 12 cents a litre. Every time a litre of gas went into a car, the federal government would have added 12 cents a litre by this petroleum compensation charge. This charge is now in excess of something like $1.5 billion. That is the figure, taking into account that there is much locked-in oil in western Canada that we have not brought out.
That extra charge is money sitting at the government's disposal, at the expense of the consumer, gaining interest for the government at a time when Canadians across the country are suffering under these increased prices. That is something which the government is prepared to unilaterally increase by an additional 24 cents a gallon by order in council. It would do the same thing with the Canadian ownership charge, which is now about $1.15 a barrel. This will provide a maximum level of about $4 a barrel. That charge is what each Canadian is paying each time a litre or a gallon of gasoline comes out of the pump. That is about four cents now. That charge, in a discretionary, in an arbitrary, even in a unilateral way, according to this clause, can be increased to a maximum of $4 a barrel.
Consumers across Canada are faced with these increased charges. They are faced with these prices that have been put in place and they are given those additional prices at the same time as the Liberal government is saying that we are going to have a fair energy policy, that we will have an energy policy that will make it right for Canadians to achieve self-sufficiency, and all these things. What have Canadians really got to show for that? What they have to show is that all the things that are really the hallmark now of the National Energy Program are really the cross that the minister has to bear. As boldly as he would like to tell Canadians that his energy program is working, the industry knows, and Canadians are gradually becoming aware, that this is a big fugue, really, that it is a con job, a job where Canadians are told one thing and precisely the opposite is happening. Capital is flowing from the country. The investors have lost confidence. Oil companies
June 3, 1982

have not been able to produce. Consumers are facing increasing prices and do not have anything to show for it. We have had a massive transfer of taxes into the federal coffers, taxes that have not increased our ability to achieve the self-sufficiency goal. In fact, last year, 1981, we had no new oil found. In spite of all the increased revenues that the federal government has got, our deficits continue to increase.
All of the negatives are there; and there is not a darned positive thing about it. There is just nothing that could give us any hope that this kind of measure, this kind of approach, will satisfy any of the claims that the minister makes for his energy program.
The Canadian Bar Association took particular exception to this clause. They suggested that any change that would be made would have to be made by consultation. We went through a long process in the country, in the opposition and the government side of the House, in dealing with the Constitution. The bottom line of that was the Supreme Court saying: "Yes, legally you can claim that right but really what we need and have to have traditionally in this country is co-operation and understanding and agreement that is reached by the provinces and agreed to by all the parties concerned." That was the legitimate response and the government finally acceded to that and we got an agreement that was in general accepted-with a notable exception.
What we are doing now is in a smaller way and in a less important way. We are saying that although the Canadian government could not do it at that level with that particular document, it does not really matter. The federal Liberal government is saying: "in spite of that, we are prepared to say here that we will do in a unilateral way whatever we please, regardless of what the producers may say, or what a producing province might say, or even what a consuming province might say; we will do it, we have the right and we are going to take the legal authority through this bill that we will pass because we have a majority in the House of Commons."
Several speakers have mentioned co-operative federalism. If there were a chance, if there were an opportunity for us to repair some of the bridges that have been nearly burned down in our relationships with the provinces, whether in the west or in the east or in central Canada, this bill will make sure we are not going to be able to restore that sense of co-operation, that sense of confidence between the provinces and the federal government, the kind of equanimity and happy relationship that we used to have and that I can remember well back in the late 1960s. That is gradually eroded each time this federal government has interfered, acted unilaterally, acted politically, in order to maintain power, in order to achieve control, in order to gain revenues, in fact, so that as a government they could become more and more involved in all of the things that are occurring in Canada. There are many things that most Canadians would like to support, but if we cannot do it in a cooperative way, if we cannot do it as a unit and as a nation, then we have lost everything.
The agreement that has been made so far took several years and caused a lot of grief. The agreements between Alberta and the federal government were agreements that ended with the
Petroleum Administration Act
system of prices and the system of increases that was laid down, that was acceptable to both parties and that Canadians in general accepted. People knew that energy prices had to go up in spite of the fact that it was a political tool, a very powerful argument for the Liberals in the last election.
Now, individual Canadian consumers are faced with all this discretionary power, orders in council and higher and higher and higher taxes and prices, that are really helping to put the crunch on the invididual Canadian. I think particularly of people in agriculture, and there are many in my constituency facing high prices for fertilizers and farm fuels; but I think it applies equally to almost any segment of Canadian economic activity. It looks as if it will get a lot worse and that it will continue to cost Canadians more and more.
The minister tries to justify and rationalize these increased costs and his energy program continually erodes, and we see with deep regret the country falling further and further behind in an international way. We saw the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) try to support the idea that it was not the energy program that was contributing in a major way to the fall of the Canadian dollar. I do not think that really washes now. Everyone knows that energy prices have caused a considerable amount of the inflationary push that we have had.
Many people know that because the money for investment in energy is gone, we have lost a lot of the interest rate reductions that we could have had. People in the areas affected directly certainly know that, because we failed at Alsands, tens of thousands of jobs are gone, lost. They know that because of the failure of Cold Lake, tens of thousands of jobs are lost. They know that the natural gas pipeline from Alaska is gone and that we have lost that. They know that there is failure after failure after failure in the energy program. No amount of argument, no amount of false bravado, can change the fact that the whole thing is in a shambles.
We need not only a major revision in the specifics of this and other bills that are part of the energy legislation, but we need a complete revision in the attitude of the government so that we can get the individual Canadians and particularly the small producers on a sound economic footing. We must restore the confidence to the business community, so that the minister and his government will have an opportunity to see that the economy starts to grow again. I do not think we can expect that out of this minister. He is completely in tune with the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). He supports his budget.
He supports all the measures the Minister of Finance has brought forward, as do all Liberal members. That is unfortunate for the Canadian people, and I hope the minister will at least accept the single suggestion in the amendment we have before us now or perhaps just the challenge of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kings way (Mr. Waddell) to explain to this side of the House that that part of this clause does not mean

what it says, that the federal government will do unilaterally what it wishes and impose on Canadian consumers, businessmen and farmers the increases allowable under this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I too am very concerned about this clause in the bill and hope we can prevail upon those who support the government to understand what the motion we have moved this evening is intended to do. What it is designed to do is take away from the cabinet the power unilaterally to revoke a pricing agreement.
I would like to speak for a moment about written agreements. I hope the minister will pay attention. A written agreement can be changed only with the consent of both parties. If the government intended to reduce taxes or prices by virtue of a new agreement, it seems to me it would have no trouble obtaining the consent of both of the parties which signed the agreement. It could bring about that change to lower prices or taxes. We are all accountable to our electorate. I think we would find it very difficult to go home to our constituents and say we had not supported lower taxes. Changes to an agreement can be made with the consent of both parties, and that seems a practical approach when it comes to reducing taxes. What the government clearly intends to do by this clause is to take unto itself the power to raise taxes unilaterally. 1 have to agree with the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) when he says, "If the government intends otherwise, 1 would like to hear from it." The best way we could hear from the government would be for it to support this amendment. Skipping the first part of the clause, it says:
-In the opinion of the governor in council, is not effective or is not capable of being effective, the governor in council may, by regulation, establish maximum prices for the various qualities and kinds of crude oil to which this part applies-
The key phrase is "not effective or is not capable of being effective". That means if it is not effective in terms of what the government intends to do with it. I am not a lawyer, but common sense tells me that clause means if it is not effective for the purposes the government intended. It does not mean it is ineffective for purposes solely of enforcement, which I could go along with, but it means it is not effective, or it can mean it is not effective in terms of the purposes the government intends for that particular excise tax.
As I have tried to point out, to me that means the government is taking upon itself the power to raise taxes. The government of the day has the power to bring bills before the House and to have them debated and passed by the House. It seems to me that is what a democratic system should be. It should be accountable to the people for taxes, for the way they are raised and paid and for the way they are dispensed with. However, this kind of clause in the bill erodes further the accountability of the parliamentary system to the people who sent us here to sit as watchdogs over their tax dollars.
I come from western Canada. Many people in my constituency are in the cattle business. Large deals, in terms of dollars, are made, although they are not large deals in terms of a farm's output. One might make a deal on the telephone whereby his word is his bond. The hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) referred to this in his opening remarks. One's word is one's bond. A person might want to sell a total
year's production of cattle and, if he has a reputation for being an honest person, he makes that kind of deal over the telephone. He can give his word, and it is his bond. I agree with the hon. member for Calgary Centre that we should go back to the day when our word meant something. However, under this bill a written agreement between parties can be changed by only one of the parties involved.
If I go to a bank for a mortgage to buy a house, I negotiate the terms of that loan. It is agreed that payments will be made over a period of two, three, four or five years-whatever term is agreed upon-at a fixed rate of interest. If I were to begin paying my mortgage and after two or three months the bank telephoned me to tell me it had decided unilaterally to raise the price of my mortgage I would not be in favour of that. Nobody would. That would be the cause of many court cases, and I would hope that kind of thing would not be allowed and that banks would be forced to honour the terms of original agreements. Yet under this clause the government is asking for the power unilaterally to change an agreement which has been arrived at.
I see the distinguished Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Dingwall) smiling. 1 hope he will take my remarks seriously. If he does not support this amendment, he will be agreeing that we have come to the point in our country where the government should have the power to change agreements it does not like unilaterally.
Two or three weeks ago we had the opportunity to talk with some people who arrange for the investment of funds in this country. In the course of the conversation the point was made that the people who deal with the investment of money in this country do not think past six months any more because after six months the rules will be changed and it will be a whole new ball game. That is a terrible statement to make and have it applicable to the country in which we live.
We are having troubles with our Canadian dollar. The situation has reached almost crisis proportions. Contrary to what the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) says, we in the opposition do not like to condemn our government. We do not like to condemn our country. We are proud of it. We want to do things which will make it productive and number one in the world. However, when we see that is not happening, we are made to feel sad. The point the Minister of Finance makes is that we should not condemn him because that causes problems. However, we should look at some of the things his government is doing, and I suggest this clause adds to insecurity and chases money out of the country. That causes problems for our dollar and problems for people who want to produce. Those problems are brought about by high interest rates. It is precisely this kind of legislation that the government is proposing that is causing these problems. When we think of what the National Energy Program and its back-in provisions have already done, we understand why nobody looks at us with any faith any more.
June 3, 1982

As I said, the people with whom 1 had an opportunity to speak said that within six months the rules will change and there will be a whole new ball game, so no one thinks beyond six months any more. Large amounts of money are leaving Canada and, by and large, going to the United States. Literally billions of dollars are being chased out of our country, and that is forcing the price of the American dollar up. One would normally think that when we sell our dollars out of the country, the price of the Canadian dollar would fall. Because we live so close to the Americans and because we are each other's best customers as far as trade is concerned, we have tried-1 think for very good reasons-to tie the Canadian dollar to the American dollar. This is a very interesting point.
I see that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) is not paying any attention. 1 think he should pay attention. I think the Minister of Finance should also pay attention. When this kind of clause serves the purpose of chasing massive amounts of Canadian dollars out of our country, that money leaving the country causes the price of the American dollar to rise. Subsequently, the price of the Canadian dollar rises with it, and this brings about an effect opposite to that which we might normally expect. It is like being in a boat that is sinking and instead of bailing it out, someone puts lead in it to make it sink faster. That is the effect that this clause will have.
I want to turn now to agriculture which is a subject that is near and dear to a lot of members from western Canada. At the present time, a tremendous amount of tax is paid on the fuel that is used for the production of food and we are already in the situation where we find it difficult to compete with the United States. 1 know we are each other's best customer, but we are also each other's closest competitor. We have to be competitive with the United States when selling our agricultural products on world markets.
I have here some figures given to me by the very distinguished hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers). They show that in 1980, a farm of approximately 1,000 acres in Alberta paid approximately $11,800 in tax on petroleum products. In 1981 that tax increased to $16,700, an increase of almost $5,000 but the frightening thing is that by 1986 it is estimated that the tax will amount to $42,000. That means a tax of $40 per acre on land for petroleum tax alone.
That is a lot of money, yet this clause provides that the tax will increase. It provides that the agreement of the parties affected can be obtained to reduce a tax, but the only way I can see the clause being used is in the case where the government wants to unilaterally increase a tax. If the bill goes through without amendment, then producers in my part of the country-and I believe the figure would be comparable for any farming area in the country-can look forward to paying taxes of more than $40 per acre simply on the fuel necessary to farm the land.
If the government does not intend that the clause will be used in the way I have outlined, I would like the minister or
Petroleum Administration Act
the parliamentary secretary to reply and point out where I am wrong. I am hoping against hope that the members of the government who represent farming regions will support the amendment. If they vote for the bill as it stands, then they are in favour of imposing a higher tax in fuel used for the production of food as the years go by.
I want to point out that this $40 per acre does not include the tax on things made from a petroleum base such as most of the insecticides, herbicides, building materials and many other products used in agriculture. That is only the tax on the fuel burned to farm the land.
In closing, I should like to emphasize an important point that was made by the hon. member for Calgary Centre. It is actually a question for a philosopher and we know that in some of his musings the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) likes to think of himself as a philosopher, so perhaps he can tussle with it. Someone said that simply because the majority is capable of doing something, that does not make it right. I took a philosophy course at university like a lot of other members and I remember that someone said simply because you have a majority and they are capable of imposing their will on the minority, that does not mean that their ability to impose their will makes it right.
Surely we must have some reason to be proud of the system that has brought this country to where it is today. This clause, however, puts us in a situation where we can simply say that because we have a majority, anything that majority does is, by definition, right. In my opinion, and I suspect in the opinion of most Canadians, that does not make it right at all. In fact, I think many people would say the opposite-that because you have the ability to impose your will on someone that does not make it right. There has to be some room for common sense and justice, otherwise we would simply be ruled by the largest and most powerful. In the same way that the government can impose its will on us because it has a majority, the people who are the biggest, the strongest or the most gifted could impose their will on the less gifted and less strong.
I urge members of the government who will support the bill to consider some of the implications of this clause if it goes through without the amendment we have put forward this evening.
I do not want to prolong the debate, Mr. Speaker, but I am glad to have had the opportunity to participate.

Mr. Speaker, most people in Canada are a little confused by the name of the riding I represent and they are not sure if I represent the whole province or a little bit of it!
I was interested when the gentleman from Etobicoke who happens to represent the riding of Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) referred to himself as a westerner. I finally understood why he went west. Being from Etobicoke he is jealous of my colleague, the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson). He could not get that riding if he wanted it. Even if he did get the nomination, he could not be elected there.
