Petroleum Administration Act
If the hon. member had been at committee with those of us who went over this bill word by word and clause by clause, he would understand what Clause 15 is about.
This motion asks that the words "in the opinion of' be deleted. As the clause stands, the minister need have no fear of not Canadianizing the oil industry because he will drive out not only foreign investment, but Canadian investment as well.
How can anyone be expected to invest in an industry where the minister can make a unilateral decision on the sale price of products? As has been mentioned before, billions of Canadians dollars have left the country in the past year. The minister was worried about foreign investment, but he does not have to worry about that.
This is totalitarian legislation. It is designed strictly for the Liberal government. It gives so much power to the minister that he can do what he wants without ever referring to his partners in confederation, the producer provinces. He could write up a contract with the producer provinces one day and next day cancel it, as soon as his bureaucrats in Ottawa got his ear and told him he did not have to go through with it.
I plead with the government to take the four words "in the opinion of' out of this clause. Make this a true partnership contract. That is what we have in Canada. I plead with the government not to try to impose its unilateral views on the citizens of this country. That is what is happening more and more with every piece of legislation.
I do not profess to be a lawyer, but I have been in the business world. I have signed many contracts, and I have done many contracts with a handshake. I will tell you one thing, Mr. Speaker, sure as the devil I would not make a contract with that government, by signature or handshake, because they have no sense of morality. They want to run it their way; they do not give a damn about Canadians or jobs for Canadians. They care only about one thing, themselves.
At least there is one member of that party who is honest. He participated in the committee, and he stood up in this House and expressed the views of the Liberal Party. He said "if we must be communists, we will be communists". At least he is honest. I respect that gentleman for saying that, because at least he told the public the truth. They do not care about the public, they care only about power, their jobs and their indexed pensions. I hope they have their six years in because the next time around they are going to have a terrible surprise.
We hear a lot of discussion in this House about rights. But what about duty, duty as Canadians, as cabinet ministers of that government? They have a duty to industry, to the ten provinces and territories. They have a duty to this country which they are not fulfilling. And I think I can explain why. The hon. member for Pontiac-Gatineau-Labelle (Mr. Lefebvre), in one of the committee meetings, happened to say "I wish we had oil wells in our backyard." My colleague, the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre), jumped on it very quickly and said "I wish to God you had those wells in
your backyard, too, if you did, we would not have this legislation in front of us". I am from the centre of this country and I object to the discrimination against the western portion of this country.
We were in committee today, and it was interesting. Hydro-Quebec and Ontario Hydro, provincial Crown corporations, came up with some changes. They were shot through right away; this is going to be changed, this is the way it is going to go. The private sector has been there and put their point across about the problems of the industry. Has the government made any changes on behalf of the industry? No, Mr. Speaker.
It will only make changes on behalf of Crown corporations and on behalf of the people its members represent. It is sad that they only represent such a small geographical portion of this country, but I understand why. It is because those people have enough common sense to not elect them to this House. I plead with hon. members opposite that when they stand up to vote, they wince as the camera goes by, because they are not helping Canada, the unity of Canada, and they are not helping Canadian citizens.

Mr. Speaker, I will not take much of the time of the House on this motion but it does stand in my name and I would like to comment on it. I would like Canadians, those in our gallery this evening and those watching us on television, to consider what their situation would be if they signed a contract with a mortgage company, for whatever term, and the mortgage company then tore up that agreement and demanded its money instantly. How many millions of Canadians would lose their homes? Where would the mortgage companies be if a customer could tear up an agreement without their consent? Would they lend you money?
Where would we be if we used a credit card to make a purchase, at a certain interest rate, and then the company could change that rate? What if you thought you borrowed money at 10 per cent, but after you borrowed it the company said no, it was at 100 per cent? Where would we be if agreements freely entered into could be broken by one side alone without consultation or process? We would have chaos. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), supported by the cabinet, is asking the elected members of this House to pass a clause which puts into jeopardy an agreement freely entered into by both parties. It gives the federal cabinet-not Parliament, not the elected representatives-an appointed group, the power to unilaterally break an agreement which they entered into on behalf of the Canadian people.
Each day in question period-I wish the minister would pay attention-he says "I cannot do this because I have an agreement with Alberta; I cannot do that because I have an agreement with Saskatchewan". I wish I could believe that. It would be so much easier to believe if he did not put in this legislation a clause which allows him to break that agreement at any time without consultation.
Even if we have faith in this cabinet and its wisdom, what about the future? What about the future for your children and my children? There will be an election sooner or later and a


*

new cabinet, and that cabinet could be sworn in at eleven o'clock in the morning and by noon it could issue a statement which completely cancelled an agreement entered into with any and all provincial governments. How would members of that party not serving in that cabinet feel? What if the Government of Canada enters into an agreement with Ontario or Quebec and that party's cabinet unilaterally abrogates that agreement? The backbenchers, people elected to represent the people of the provinces concerned, have no say.
It is just the cabinet, based on what information no one knows, because cabinet meetings are secret. We are dealing with principle. Our society runs in large measure on the fact that we have agreements with each other and that we mutually change agreements. We do not have the principle where two parties as matters of free choice enter into written agreements with each other that can be broken by one party.
When the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) stands in his place in this chamber, either during question period or at any other time, and says that he cannot do something because he has an agreement with another province, then we will know if this clause passes without amendment that that is a charade because the minister will have given himself the power to break any agreement. When he says that he cannot do something because an agreement is in place, what he would be saying to us is that he chooses to do something or chooses not to do something.
Simply, this clause says that the Canadian people cannot trust their federal government to keep an agreement, an agreement which it entered into on their behalf. This is awesome power the minister has. The minister was asked about that in committee. On that occasion he gave no clear indication why the clause was in the bill. We asked him why he wanted that power. We really did not get an answer. We asked him whether that clause was put in the bill by accident or by design of some civil servant. The minister did not really know.
We suggested that he take this clause out of the bill and that if he needed it later on that he should have the courage to come before Parliament, before the elected people, and defend the need to have the unilateral power to tear up an agreement with the provinces. If something like that is ever necessary, there is a proper forum and place in which to do it. But why does the minister need this power at this time, given the uncertainties that exist in Canada today and the stresses on our confederation? Surely we should not have a clause that encourages the present minister, or any future minister, to act unilaterally without consultation and be able to tear up an agreement that was entered into.
Agreements should be changed through mutual negotiation. Agreements should not be one-sided. In that context, I encourage those members who support the principle that agreements should be changed as a consequence of negotiation to vote for this amendment. The only members of this chamber who should vote against this amendment are those who really believe it is right to give the cabinet the power, without
Petroleum Administration Act
complication, to tear up an agreement made with another member of this confederation. That is not right. The House should indicate that in the strongest possible way. It is not an issue on which government's fall, but it is an issue of principle and this chamber should support the principle that lies behind the amendment.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be brief. However, I do not want to leave unanswered on the record certain allegations that have been made tonight. I listened carefuly to the comments made on this particular amendment by the hon. member who has just spoken and by some of his predecessors. By listening to what they said, you would believe that what is being proposed here, as the hon. member mentioned, is that the governor in council, the cabinet, could at will tear up an agreement reached with a particular province concerning oil prices, an agreement that would have been arrived at freely. You would believe that this is a new provision, a new power which the government is trying to get for itself.
First, I would like to point out that the provision of the bill states that when there is no agreement, the governor in council, the cabinet, can by regulation establish maximum prices for various kinds of crude oil. Or, again, if there is an agreement and the agreement is terminated by the declaration of the parties, again, the governor in council can promulgate prices by regulation.
That is the point to which the hon. member who last spoke is objecting. It says that "where the agreement is not effective or not capable of being effective-", which in French reads: "Lorsque .. . I'accord conclu nest pas executoire ou n'est pas susceptible de Ie devenir."
What does that mean? It means that if there is an agreement and it cannot be implemented or cannot be acted upon because of circumstances beyond the control of the parties, then the cabinet, the governor in council, can establish maximum prices for crude oil if there was an agreement that for whatever reason could not be implemented, could not be made effective. Some members have said that this would destroy the confidence in the industry. As I indicated, you would think this is a brand new provision which this government is trying to get to allow it to walk away from agreements made with any particular province. I would like to remind my hon. friends on the other side, who may not have paid attention to this provision as much as they should have, that this is not a new provision. This very provision is Section 36 of the Petroleum Administration Act and it has been there ever since 1975 when that act was passed by Parliament.
That doesn't make it right.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Let me read this section from Bill C-47, the Petroleum Administration Act. It reads:
Where no agreement is entered into pursuant to Section 22 with the government of a producer-province, or any such agreement is terminated by the declaration of the parties, or, in the opinion of the governor in council, is not effective or is not capable of being effective, the governor in council may, by

June 3, 1982
Petroleum Administration Act
regulation, establish maximum prices for the various qualities and kinds of crude oil to which this part applies that are produced, extracted or recovered in that province.
That is section 23(1) here, word for word. It is simply reproduced because Sections 34 to 46 of Bill C-47, the Petroleum Administration Act, have been repeated. There is nothing new or anything that is frightening for the industry.
I would remind my hon. friends that the industry has known its golden years with respect to money and other matters with that provision. That provision had been examined by parliamentary committees, debated, voted and passed by Parliament in 1975. Therefore, all the agitation of my hon. friends in the Tory benches, I would have to say, is somewhat fabricated. If it is not fabricated, it took them seven years to become that outraged. I would invite them to go back to the bill which has been in effect since 1975. There is nothing changed. Nothing has been changed in this case either.
It is wrong, then.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
The hon. member says that it is wrong, then. I would remind him that his government was in office for nine months. If this was such a terrible detriment to the west, as I heard some of them say, why did they not introduce an amendment to this bill when they were in office, even for first reading?
I am not asking them to have passed a bill, since they did not have much time to do that, but they could have at least indicated the seriousness of their concern over this provision by introducing an amendment in Parliament indicating that they did not like this provision of the Petroleum Administration Act. They could have said, "We think it is outrageous and therefore we will quickly table, at least, an amendment for first reading."
They did not do that. I would suggest it was not because they did not have the time since it would have been a very easy amendment to draft. They did not do it because there is nothing very outrageous about it. It is a very simple and explainable provision. It is quite understandable because we must bear in mind that there may be special circumstances when a certain agreement with a certain province may become ineffective or unable to be implemented. As the government of the nation, it must have the power to assume its responsibility in the national interest and act to ensure that the prices for various kinds of crude oil will be determined at a time when a certain agreement for a particular reason becomes ineffective.
It is my hope that these few points will have at least removed the notion from the minds of my hon. friends that there is some secret plot which was suddenly invented in the last few months whereby the government and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources would be accumulating new powers that no one has ever heard of. Even the Conservative minister of energy, when he was in office, had this power and lived with it. The country did not suffer from it. On the contrary, I think it is a precautionary clause which is quite
understandable and which has not given rise to arguments even from the producing provinces. I can tell hon. members that in two years this point has not been raised once with me by any particular provincial minister of energy.
Why?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Why? Because, I am happy to say, the provincial ministers of energy appear to have more sense and have been a little more reasonable with these issues than some members opposite who have spoken tonight.
I do not want to spend any time on some of the more despicable remarks made by the hon. member for Calgary Centre (M. Andre). I think they were very well answered by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell). I will simply say that I regret that members of the House feel they have to resort to this kind of argument during a debate. I do not believe they are serving their cause and they are not serving themselves. They are not growing in their own minds by using that kind of argument or in the minds of the public. I do not believe that they serve the cause of understanding, tolerance and friendship between the various regions of this country which is so important.
I only want to say that the arguments that were used did not appropriately reflect the provisions of the bill which were being discussed. These provisions regarding taxation, particularly in the transportation field, will apply equally to foreign as well as domestic carriers. With respect to the hon. member who spent much time discussing maritime transportation, it has been made quite clear before the committee and barely needs to be repeated here that those provisions are not discriminatory against Canadian carriers or transporters. They apply equally to foreign as well as Canadian carriers. I reject those arguments which have been made.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to briefly respond to the remarks made by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) in regard to this portion of the bill which deals with the agreement. This agreement is very important to the industry today because the major problem facing the industry is a lack of confidence. This is just one more area where that confidence breaks down; the minister's right to break the agreement at his discretion. These powers given to the minister adds to the breakdown of confidence.
I sat in the committee for the past two years and listened to witnesses who appeared before that committee. Contrary to what the minister says, the matter of confidence was raised as the number one subject. I believe it was the Elf Aquitaine Company of France which said, with reference to Bill C-48 in particular, that they had never seen this type of legislation introduced in the free world which would allow confiscation as it did under Bill C-48.
In this clause we have the exact same kind of powers of discretion by the minister. If we realistically look at what has to happen in Canada today in order to restore confidence in
June 3, 1982

the National Energy Program and to get investment returning to Canada with respect to the National Energy Program, it is this very matter which must be dealt with. The timing of this was very important because of the actions of the minister with regard to the National Energy Program. That is the point which was being made by the hon. member who spoke previously and to whom the minister referred. It is most important that confidence be restored to the industry so it can depend on the government and on signed contracts.
If you consider the situation as it relates to the falling Canadian dollar today, I would suggest to Canadians and to the minister that the main reason for the weakening Canadian dollar is the National Energy Program and the lack of confidence that the minister himself has brought upon a very successful industry in Canada through the kind of directions he has given to the National Energy Program.
This bill is no exception and this is why it is so important. I would just like to say briefly, in these closing remarks, that I must respond to the minister. It is most important that this ordinary discretion on the part of the minister not be taken at this time to further weaken confidence in an industry that must go ahead in developing our resources. This country should be number one and should not be falling behind in the economic situation as we are today.
Hear, hear!

Petroleum Administration Act
That Bill C-103, An Act to amend the Petroleum Administration Act and to enact provisions related thereto be amended in Clause 16 by striking out line 19 at page 12 and substituting the following therefor:
"(d) the probable effect on the explorers, producers".
He said: Mr. Speaker, I would simply like to refer to Motion No. 3 in its context. What we are asking or what precedes this amendment is the power of cabinet to set price. The motion that was brought forward by the minister-and we challenged it in committee-is the clause appearing in the bill and it asserts that in the setting of price, the cabinet should be concerned about the impact of that price on consumers and producers. What we seek to do through our amendment tonight is to change one word, and that is "explorers", because if we have learned with a sense of clarity what this minister's policy has done, we can see it so clearly in the exploration end of the business. Today in Canada one quarter of the wells being drilled were being drilled before that man became Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde).
In that period of time he has single-handedly destroyed three quarters of the exploration industry in this country. He has destroyed hundreds of family-owned, small firms which have gone into bankruptcy. He has caused people to lose their jobs and, subsequently, their homes. He has put the energy future of all of us at risk because the oil and gas industry begins by looking for the needle in the haystack.
Buried somewhere in the ground is a pool of oil or a reservoir of gas. We have technical ways of guessing where it might be, but then one needs half a million dollars to even drill a shallow well. Most wells would cost at least $1 million. Someone has to pay that money. One hires a drilling rig, hires truckers, caterpillar tractors, cooks, builds shacks and then one drills. One finds oil and gas or one does not find oil or gas. More frequently, one does not, but it takes much money and it is a high-stakes, high-risk venture. It takes money.
But this minister, through his National Energy Program, took the money away from the people who know how to look for oil and gas and two years later we have less of it. By analogy, if this minister had taken over a grocery store, bought it on behalf of the Canadian people, he would have started selling the groceries off the shelves, taken the money, gone somewhere and had a party.
Do hon. members know what the first use of the money should have been put to? It should have gone to the wholesalers to put the groceries back on the shelves for the next customers. But when one does not do that, but just sells the groceries and does not buy more with the money to put back on the shelves, pretty soon every shelf in the store is empty. That is what would happen and that is what the minister has done to this country.
Governments take 65 cents out of every dollar Canadians pay for oil and gas. There is not enough left in that 35 cents to look for oil and gas. So, we force them to sell it. We are selling the groceries off our shelves. This minister will not leave the industry enough money to drill the wells, to put that oil "back on the shelves" for the next generation, for your kids and for

my kids. In the process of doing that, he has caused all kinds of small, family-owned firms to go into bankruptcy.
Last week, the biggest auction sale in the history of western Canada was held, selling drilling rigs, caterpillar tractors, trucks, equipment, and the buyers were Americans, citizens of the United States of America. The prices were less than halfprice. The minister stood in this House on Monday night, some three or four days after that auction sale, and said, "We will update the program". What did he brag about? He bragged about giving the oil industry $2 billion more. That is the way he said it. But what he really meant was that he would take $2 billion less away from them.
They found the oil and the money was theirs. With his taxation policies, he took too much away. He took so much away that we cannot drill the holes any more. We cannot find the oil. We are burning it. It is burning in this building right now. It is burning in all those cars out on the street. But there is no well drilling to replace it. It is going. Less than 100 wells are being drilled in this whole country-
Ninety-four, to be exact.

-on this day. We were up to 700, 800 or 900 in the course of a month, but this minister has taken away the future from your children and my children, at least in part. He is taking so much of the money that there is not enough left to hire the people to drill the wells. He stands in this chamber and tells us that we have an agreement with the provinces and that if we go out and find new oil, we will get the world price. Canadians believe him and the newspapers carry the headlines.
Then we read in Clause 16 that he can tear that agreement up on 30 seconds' notice. "Take your money today," he says to Canadians, "invest in an oil rig and go drill a well, and if you find it, you will get a certain price." But hidden in the legislation which his members intend to vote for is the principle that what he tells you today, he can break tomorrow without your consent, without your advice. That is what creates the instability. People do not trust.
The minister told us on Monday night that the energy program had accomplished great things and that it was going to do better things. Well, since Monday night we have stood in this House and said: "No, you have made it a little better than it was, but it is still rotten, it is still bad." The report card will be what happens on the stock exchange and what happens to the value of the dollar. Since Monday night, all stocks have gone down 200 points and the dollar has dropped for the first time in Canadian history, below 80 cents.
Knowledgeable people in Canada have judged this minister and his so-called revision. The program was rotten. It was revised. Canadians have said it is still rotten and it should be dropped. At the very least, I urge members of this chamber to add the simple word "explorers" so that when this minister or
some future minister determines the price and taxes, there will be some protection for our kids, that we not sell the groceries today without replacing them, but have to take into consideration in price the need to drill more wells to replace the oil we are burning.
Hear, hear!

I hope constituents listening to our discussion this evening will telephone their Members of Parliament and tell them whether they think they should vote for 48 cents when they were sent here to keep the tax under 18 cents. I hope that happens to members of the New Democratic Party too. I invite constituents to pick up their telephones tomorrow, telephone their Members of Parliament, Liberal or NDP, and tell them to vote for Motion No. 4 because it would restrict the taxing power of the minister to something less than 18 cents a gallon, and that would be in line with the brochures, pamphlets and advertising distributed and the speeches made by hon. members opposite.
I think it is generous of the Conservative Party of Canada to give hon. members in this chamber the opportunity to keep a campaign promise in this way. I hope hon. members will give a lot of thought to this at the weekend. They were sent here to uphold a principle, and by voting for this amendment they can uphold that principle with clarity, pride and dignity. However, if they choose to uphold the minister's desire for a 48 cents a gallon tax-just this one tax alone-surely they are breaking faith with the people who sent them here and the things they told them in December, 1979, in January, 1980, and in early February, 1981. That is the first half of the amendment, and I urge its consideration at the weekend.
The second half of the amendment would protect consumers. It would impose a maximum tax of 18 cents a gallon. That would be a break for the consumer. It would bring the price of gas at the pumps down right away. It would be cheaper. If the House voted for this amendment, gasoline and home heating oil would cost consumers less.
However, there is another principle, and the minister has enunciated it. He told us in committee that the petroleum compensation charge, according to his agreement with the producing provinces, shall not be set at a level greater than that required, so that the amount of money coming in through taxation and the amount paid out to Saudi Arabia and Mexico for imported oil would be the same. That is what the minister told us. However, I say to the consumers of Canada that they should beware. The minister has told consumers about his intentions, but nowhere in the wording of the clause is the minister restricted. Many times in the last few years we have been told by ministers that taxes were being levied for specific purposes, and as soon as Parliament has granted those taxing powers, the money has been used for other purposes. Through this amendment we are seeking to protect the consumers of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Being a member of the Standing Committee on Energy Legislation, I heard everything the hon. member had to say on this subject. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that enough is enough.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Conservative Party I would like to thank the hon. member for reminding Canadians that, yes, they have had enough. We have had enough of this minister, and we have had enough of this policy. I thank the hon. member for bringing this so forcefully to the attention of all Canadians.
Motion No. 4 says that the minister absolutely shall not charge more than 18 cents a gallon tax for compensation purposes. Motion No. 5 says he shall never tax at a rate greater than that required to provide compensation. If we had a decent policy under which wells were being drilled and no oil had to be imported, we would come to the point where this whole tax would disappear and it would be guaranteed in legislation that once the need had passed, the tax would no longer be collected. That is what Motion No. 5 would ensure. Motion No. 4 says there will be a maximum tax of 18 cents. Motion No. 5 says when the need is passed, which surely will happen, the government cannot collect the tax.
Surely a sane and sensible government would not collect a tax which is not needed, but I remind hon. members that in 1975 this Parliament approved an export charge. The purpose of that export charge was to pay for imports. It is now 1982, and this government is collecting that export charge and not putting a penny into paying for imports. It has a new charge of 48 cents a gallon, and there is no restriction in legislation which says it must be used for a specific purpose. There is no restriction in legislation which says that when the need is passed, the tax will disappear.
What we have here is a public relations exercise. People want this Parliament to approve taxes for good reasons, but the government does not want to restrict itself, through legislation, to those good reasons.
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

HOUSING-CMHC ROLE IN RENEWING MORTGAGES ON UREA FORMALDEHYDE FOAM INSULATED HOUSES. (B) REQUEST THAT BANKS BE INSTRUCTED TO RENEW MORTGAGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 15, as reported at page 14994 of Hansard, I inquired about CMHC guaranteeing mortgages on homes insulated with UFFI. The answer I received at that time was not satisfactory, nor could it be called positive. On April 30 I asked the same question, in effect, as reported at page 16780 of Hansard. In the reply I was assured that Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation would guarantee all applications for renewal of mortgages, but I guess I specified banks particularly and not the general mortgage industry.

June 3, 1982

Since that time I have received reports that owners of houses with UFFI insulation are still having difficulty renewing their mortgages. Today I suggested to the minister that the government should spend some of its advertising money for this purpose. Someone interjected that it would perhaps be as valuable for the home owner as advertising the Canada goose! This in no way reflects on the Canada goose-I think it is a wonderful bird and I admire it. However, I think the Canadian public would get more value from money spent advertising that CMHC will guarantee any mortgage renewal request for any house in Canada insulated with UFFI.
The decline in the value of homes insulated with this material is seriously underestimated by the government. 1 do not think it understands the problem at all. It has been publicly stated that 80 to 90 per cent of the estates of most retiring people is constituted in the value of the home they own. It is also estimated that approximately 80,000 Canadian homes have insulation containing health hazardous formaldehyde.
An article in the Ottawa Citizen of May 4 states that about
3,000	people are seeking cuts in property taxes because of foam insulation. Another article in the Ottawa Citizen on April 30 carried the heading "Ottawa fears tax loss from foam insulation". The article states that the assessment review court decided that some Sault Ste. Marie homes were worth about half their previous value, and it cut the tax bills accordingly. The article states that it will be months before it is possible to process the appeals to the assessor in respect of the taxation to be paid this year. For many families, 80 per cent to 90 per cent of the value of the estate will virtually disappear because the houses they own have little if any value.
The minister told me that if I could give him a name, he would investigate the case. If the minister is interested, he will not have any difficulty finding out about one member of this House who has an interest in one of these homes. He needed a little security and when he sought a loan through a mortgage with the house as security, he was turned down cold. He was told that in effect they would rather lend him money without security than on the security of a home with UFFI insulation. This is a measure of the serious loss experienced by people who have used this insulation.
1 have in my hand a document entitled "Urea Formaldehyde Foam Checklist". This checklist was to be handed to an occupant by the installer before the foam was installed. I have polled people in my constituency on whether they ever saw this form or anything like it. Directions for its use list several of the precautions that should have been exercised before urea formaldehyde foam insulation was installed in any home. It was supposed to assure that people would get a high quality insulation job. In part, it reads as follows:
-the contractor is required to provide you, the consumer, with an information brochure before commencing the insulation ... the onus for the manufacture and installation of urea formaldehyde foam insulation is on the contractor.
Allergy-prone people or asthmatics may be more sensitive to formaldehyde fumes and should consult their doctor before selecting this type of insulation.
Adjournment Debate
Two of my constituents have suffered as a result of being unfamiliar with this direction from the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. Section A(l) of the checklist
says:
The materials to be used should have a Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) acceptance number.
These were the directions issued by the government. It goes
on:
The contractor must have a licence bearing his/her photograph; ask to see it.
All circuits with electrical wiring carrying 200 volts or more, in any of the cavities to be foamed, must be turned off.
Every clothes dryer or stove properly installed in Canada carries 200 volts or more. It gives a guide to temperatures. The material should not be installed in attics, or in homes with a vapour barrier outside the insulation. My home has; it is just fortunate that I did not use UFFI because I would have it inside an excellent vapour barrier. I could go on.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: HOUSING-CMHC ROLE IN RENEWING MORTGAGES ON UREA FORMALDEHYDE FOAM INSULATED HOUSES. (B) REQUEST THAT BANKS BE INSTRUCTED TO RENEW MORTGAGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 30 the hon. member asked a very straightforward question:
Is it the policy of the minister responsible for housing that the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation should guarantee all applications for renewal of mortgages for UFFI homes. If it is the policy of the government, has CMHC been so instructed and are they so behaving?
The minister answered in an equally straightforward
fashion:
Madam Speaker, the answer is yes.
It is very important to make that point, that CMHC is prepared to continue to guarantee mortgages on UFFI homes and provide guarantees on mortgage renewals for such homes even if no guarantee previously existed. It is very important to establish that fact for the understanding of the hon. member and those interested in this issue.
The major banks approve their mortgage renewals, provided the borrower has a good financial record. Most of the time the banks do not inquire whether a home has UFFI or not. They look at the financial record of the home owner when considering renewal. On the other hand, when the banks do learn of the presence of UFFI they know, as the hon. member has pointed out, that the home is potentially subject to devaluation. Because it is a financial transaction, they are then much more hesitant to make a loan to the full amount of the mortgage. On that basis they ask for a guarantee, and it is on that basis that the minister pointed out that CMHC is prepared to offer that guarantee. We all realize that we must give these home owners some assistance. As the minister has pointed out, CMHC is prepared to give that assistance. That is a very laudable position of both the minister and CMHC.

June 3, 1982
Adjournment Debate

subtopic: THE ECONOMY-CLOSURE OF LUMBER MILL IN CHEMAINUS, B.C.-PROTECTION FOR JOBS. (B) INVESTMENT OF CAPITAL OUTSIDE OF CANADA
THE ECONOMY-CLOSURE OF LUMBER MILL IN CHEMAINUS, B.C.-PROTECTION FOR JOBS. (B) INVESTMENT OF CAPITAL OUTSIDE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in late April MacMillan Bloedel announced the indefinite closure of its lumber mill at Chemainus, British Columbia. Since that time the company has indicated that it has no plans to either reopen the existing mill or proceed with earlier plans to build a new mill.
The mill manager was quoted in the local newspaper as saying that the new mill would not be built now because all available capital was needed for the building of a new pulp mill in Alabama. Consequently, people in my riding face a loss of 600 jobs in the basic industry. Today happens to be the last pay day for these employees. They get exactly one day's pay and after that they can look forward to the very uncertain future of unemployment insurance. Job loss has a multiple effect, the same as job creation.
In addition to the loss of 600 jobs in the Chemainus mill, there is a loss of jobs in small supporting industries, local shops and services. A shopkeeper pointed to the psychological factor involved when a major industry shuts down. Even people who still hold their jobs cut back on their purchases because of growing uncertainty. Certainly the depressed condition of the forest industry is a factor in the Chemainus closure. British Columbia suffers today because it has become totally dependent upon the export of raw resources. As a result, British Columbia is even more vulnerable to international markets than it would be if it had a more diversified economy.
Just this past weekend in the southern part of my riding in the View Royal area, Plumper Bay Sawmills has just announced bankruptcy. The bankruptcy story is becoming far too common in the entire forest industry of British Columbia.
The International Woodworkers of America union has pointed out that at the end of May 12,837 woodworkers or 25.7 per cent of the membership were laid off. This is an increase from 8,170 people who were laid off at the end of April. Anyone who knows anything about the lumber industry in British Columbia knows that springtime is the very time when loggers are getting back to work. However, at present they are facing increased lay-offs instead.
The B.C. Central Credit Union has pointed out that some S31 million a week is being paid out for unemployment insurance in British Columbia, and it predicts that total UIC payments in B.C. could run to $2 billion by the end of the year. The $522 million budgeted by the provincial government for welfare payments will not be enough unless conditions improve. And so we recognize the general problems of the British Columbia forest industry.
MacMillan Bloedel is not immune to these problems. However, MacMillan Bloedel has not acted in the long-term interests of the community at Chemainus. The lumber mill at Chemainus has been owned by different companies for over 120 years. There was a time when the present mill was one of
the largest and most modern in the world. It was geared to cut the large and beautiful timber which grew on the east coast of Vancouver Island. It is a tragic fact that the largest and best of that timber has now been creamed by lumber companies such as MacMillan Bloedel.
The mill is now outdated and poor forestry practices in the past have caught up with the industry. British Columbians are having to pay while companies like MacMillan Bloedel take the money and run. The mill became outdated. The plant ran down and become antiquated. It did not gear up to cut the second growth timber and the smaller timber which was farther back in the hills.
Our party believes that if the multinational corporations are going to be making money from the resources of our province they should be investing their money in those provinces and creating permanent jobs.
When I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) about the export of money to build a new mill in Alabama, his only answer was that he would take notice of it. We not only face a crisis in Chemainus, not only in the forest industry of British Columbia, but across Canada. The tragedy which the people face in Chemainus is one that is shared by hundreds of thousands of Canadians. We face a government that is incapable, unwilling, or both, to take action.
In this adjournment debate, I ask the government once again if it is willing to take some action to ensure that multinational corporations will act responsibly and that they will have the welfare of the communities in which they operate in mind and not simply cream our resources, take the money and run off to exploit some other part of the world.

speakeroldname: Mr. Andre Maltais (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: THE ECONOMY-CLOSURE OF LUMBER MILL IN CHEMAINUS, B.C.-PROTECTION FOR JOBS. (B) INVESTMENT OF CAPITAL OUTSIDE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 shall try to give the hon. member a brief but nevertheless complete answer. First, the Canadian lumber industry is going through a difficult period right now, because the market is cyclical and demand is dropping in most parts of Canada and in the rest of the world, especially in countries that have their own lumber industries. Second, MacMillan Bloedel has invested over $650 million in Canada between 1979 and 1981. Third, the Alabama plant was built strictly with American funds, so there is no question of Canadian capital being drained to the United States. The plant is a sawmill built exclusively with American money. Fourth, what can be done now to help people who are laid off? I would have a great deal to say about the matter to the hon. member, because my own riding includes Baie-Comeau and Chute-aux-Outardes, both heavily dependent on the lumber industry, and we have problems there too. The Minister of the Environment and Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Roberts) and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) have signed agreements with the government of British Columbia to provide
June 3, 1982

assistance for workers by bringing in specific projects that will directly help the people who are affected by these lay-offs. The agreements were signed not only with British Columbia, but also with Ontario and other provinces, and now we must wait and see whether the action taken by the federal government is a satisfactory response to provincial needs. Fifth, the hon. member is asking the minister whether we are going to take action to ensure that the multinationals are doing whatever they can and that they are truly working in the interests of Canadians.
Adjournment Debate
I would therefore ask the hon. member whether he actually has some specific cases in which he can prove that the multinationals are taking advantage of the present situation, and if so, to let us know so that we can investigate the matter.
